docs.title: Microeconomics: An Intelligent Textbook
docs.text:
Prof. Sharat Batra · University of Minnesota · batra052@umn.edu

Welcome to Microeconomics: An Intelligent Textbook — an open, interactive course resource designed for undergraduate students at the University of Minnesota and beyond.

This textbook covers the core principles of microeconomics through clear explanations, real-world examples, mathematical models, and interactive simulations. Each chapter builds on the last, taking you from the foundational ideas of scarcity and choice all the way to international trade and behavioral economics.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• How individuals and firms make decisions under scarcity
  • How markets coordinate supply and demand to set prices
  • How different market structures (competition, monopoly, oligopoly) affect outcomes
  • How markets can fail and what policy can do about it
  • How insights from psychology reshape our understanding of economic behavior

docs.title: ECON 1101: Principles of Microeconomics
docs.text: Instructor: Prof. Sharat Batra Institution: University of Minnesota Contact: batra052@umn.edu

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text: This course introduces the fundamental principles of microeconomics — the study of how individuals, households, and firms make decisions in the face of scarcity, and how these decisions interact through markets. Students will develop analytical tools to understand resource allocation, price determination, market structure, and government policy.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates, typically first- or second-year students, with no prior economics coursework required.

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
This course is an introduction to microeconomics — the behavior of individual households, firms, and markets. The following related topics are explicitly out of scope and are left to other courses:

  • Macroeconomics (GDP, inflation, unemployment, monetary and fiscal policy)
  • Econometrics and statistical/empirical methods
  • Advanced general equilibrium theory and formal welfare theorems
  • International finance and exchange-rate economics
  • Financial markets and asset pricing

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After this course, students will be able to demonstrate competencies at each level of the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
• Define key terms including opportunity cost, marginal utility, price elasticity, consumer and producer surplus, deadweight loss, and Nash equilibrium.
  • Recall the standard assumptions of perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly.
  • Identify the major types of market failure (externalities, public goods, asymmetric information) and the standard policy tools used to address each.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
• Explain how changes in supply or demand shift market equilibrium and affect price and quantity.
  • Describe the distinguishing features of perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly, and how each determines price and output.
  • Summarize how asymmetric information creates adverse selection and moral hazard problems in markets.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
• Apply the core economic concepts of scarcity, opportunity cost, and marginal analysis to everyday and business decisions.
  • Model supply, demand, and market equilibrium graphically and mathematically, including the effects of taxes, subsidies, and price controls.
  • Apply game-theoretic reasoning (dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium) to predict outcomes in oligopoly and other strategic settings.
  • Apply marginal analysis to a firm's factor-market hiring decisions (e.g., labor demand under different market structures).

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
• Analyze how different market structures affect prices, output, and social welfare.
  • Analyze how price, income, and cross-price elasticity affect the incidence of taxes and subsidies between buyers and sellers.
  • Analyze how asymmetric information (adverse selection, moral hazard, signaling) distorts market outcomes relative to the competitive benchmark.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
• Evaluate the causes and consequences of market failures, including externalities, public goods, and imperfect information.
  • Evaluate policy trade-offs such as tariffs versus free trade, and Pigouvian taxes versus cap-and-trade, using efficiency and equity criteria.
  • Evaluate the welfare implications of different forms of price discrimination and market power.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
• Design and justify a policy proposal that addresses a specific market failure (e.g., a negative externality or a public good), using supply-and-demand and welfare analysis to support the recommendation.
  • Construct an original numerical or graphical model of a market scenario (e.g., a new tax, a price ceiling, or an oligopoly pricing game) and justify the assumptions used.
  • Create an explainer (short report, infographic, or presentation) that teaches a real-world market scenario to a non-expert audience using at least three microeconomic models or frameworks from the course.

Note

docs.title: What is ECON 1101 about, and who is it designed for?
docs.text: ECON 1101, Principles of Microeconomics, is an introductory course taught by Prof. Sharat Batra at the University of Minnesota. It studies how individuals, households, and firms make decisions in the face of scarcity, and how those decisions interact through markets to determine prices, output, and the allocation of resources. The course is designed for college undergraduates, typically first- or second-year students, and assumes no prior economics coursework. You will learn the core toolkit economists use to analyze everyday and business decisions: scarcity and opportunity cost, supply and demand, consumer and producer behavior, market structures from perfect competition to monopoly, strategic (game-theoretic) reasoning, factor markets like labor, and the causes and remedies of market failure. For example, the course will equip you to explain not just that gasoline prices rose, but why, using the same demand-and-supply framework that applies to concert tickets, rental apartments, or coffee beans. The course closes with two "frontiers" units, behavioral economics and international trade, that connect classical theory to real human behavior and to the global economy. By the end, you will be able to read a supply-and-demand graph, reason through a strategic business decision, and evaluate a public policy proposal using the same analytical tools professional economists use. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: Do I need any prior economics background to take this course?
docs.text: No. ECON 1101 is built from the ground up for students with zero prior exposure to economics. The course description explicitly states that no prior economics coursework is required, and Chapter 1 begins with first-principles definitions of economics, scarcity, and choice before building any formal models. What you do need is basic algebra, since the course relies on graphs, slopes, and simple equations (for example, finding where a demand line and a supply line cross). Calculus appears only in optional advanced sections and is never required to pass the course or complete the standard practice problems. If you have taken a high school economics class, you will recognize some vocabulary, but the course does not assume you remember any of it, and it redefines every term precisely using the glossary and in-chapter definitions rather than assuming prior familiarity. For example, a student who has never heard the phrase "opportunity cost" will get a full, example-driven introduction to it in the first chapter before it is used again anywhere else in the book. The main prerequisite is simply a willingness to think carefully about trade-offs and to work through graphs and word problems methodically. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: How is the textbook organized into chapters and units?
docs.text: The textbook has 16 chapters organized into 6 units that build on one another in sequence. Unit 1, Foundations (Chapters 1 to 3), covers scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, supply and demand, and elasticity. Unit 2, Consumer and Producer Theory (Chapters 4 to 5), covers how consumers maximize utility and how firms choose production levels and incur costs. Unit 3, Market Structures (Chapters 6 to 10), is the largest unit and walks through perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, and game theory in that order, since each structure builds on ideas from the one before it. Unit 4, Factor Markets (Chapter 11), applies the same marginal reasoning to labor and capital markets. Unit 5, Market Failures and Policy (Chapters 12 to 14), covers externalities, public goods, and information problems. Unit 6, Frontiers of Microeconomics (Chapters 15 to 16), covers behavioral economics and international trade. Because later chapters depend on earlier ones (for example, Chapter 7 on monopoly assumes you already understand marginal revenue and cost curves from Chapter 6), the book is designed to be read roughly in order rather than skipped around. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What math background do I need for this course?
docs.text: You need basic algebra: solving linear equations, working with slopes and intercepts, reading and plotting points on a graph, and doing straightforward percentage calculations. These skills are used constantly, for instance when finding the equilibrium price and quantity where a demand equation and a supply equation are equal, or when computing a price elasticity using percentage changes in price and quantity. Calculus (derivatives) appears only in optional advanced sections of a few chapters, such as deriving marginal cost from a total cost function, and it is never required for the core learning objectives, the standard practice problems, or the quizzes. If your algebra is rusty, the main thing to review before starting is how to solve two linear equations simultaneously (substitution or setting them equal to each other), since this is exactly the skill used to find market equilibrium in Chapter 2 and is reused throughout the book. For example, if demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 20 + 3P, setting them equal and solving for P is the same algebra skill used again and again in cost curves, elasticity formulas, and factor market problems. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What topics does this course NOT cover?
docs.text: ECON 1101 is deliberately scoped to microeconomics, the behavior of individual households, firms, and markets, and it explicitly leaves several related topics to other courses. It does not cover macroeconomics, meaning GDP, inflation, unemployment, or monetary and fiscal policy; it does not cover econometrics or statistical and empirical research methods; it does not cover advanced general equilibrium theory or formal welfare theorems; and it does not cover international finance, exchange-rate economics, or financial markets and asset pricing. If you are looking for a course on how the Federal Reserve sets interest rates, why national unemployment rises and falls, or how to value a stock portfolio, those belong in a macroeconomics or finance course rather than this one. This course's international trade chapter (Chapter 16) focuses on the microeconomic side of trade, comparative advantage, tariffs, and who wins and loses from trade, rather than exchange rates or the balance of trade's macroeconomic effects. Knowing this scope upfront helps you set the right expectations: this is a course about individual decision-making and market outcomes, not about the economy-wide aggregates covered in a principles of macroeconomics course. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What are MicroSims, and where do I find them in each chapter?
docs.text: MicroSims are interactive, browser-based simulations embedded directly in the textbook that let you manipulate a model and watch the results change in real time, rather than just reading about them. For example, instead of only reading that a leftward shift in supply raises equilibrium price, a MicroSim lets you drag a slider that shifts the supply curve and watch the equilibrium point move on the graph immediately. They are used throughout the book wherever a concept is genuinely hard to grasp from text and a static diagram alone, such as visualizing a payoff matrix in game theory, exploring how marginal cost and average cost curves interact, or seeing how a tariff changes consumer and producer surplus. Each MicroSim lives in its own page under the book's sims/ section and is embedded inside the relevant chapter where that concept is introduced. MicroSims carry a status indicator (a colored dot) showing whether they are still a scaffold, fully built, or author-approved for learners; most sims you encounter in finished chapters will be built or approved. You are encouraged to actually interact with each MicroSim as you reach it rather than skipping past it, since manipulating the model yourself builds intuition that passive reading cannot. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What does a typical chapter include?
docs.text: Every chapter in this textbook follows the same consistent structure so you always know what to expect. Each chapter opens with a list of Learning Objectives stating exactly what you should be able to do after finishing it, phrased using action verbs like "explain," "apply," or "evaluate." The main body is organized into numbered sections containing explanatory text, worked examples, diagrams, and, where algebra is involved, the relevant math written out step by step. Interactive MicroSims appear at the points where a concept benefits from hands-on exploration rather than only text. A Key Terms section near the end defines the chapter's important vocabulary, which also appears in the book-wide glossary. Finally, each chapter ends with Practice Problems, exercises with worked solutions that let you test whether you actually absorbed the material before moving to the next chapter. You will also notice recurring mascot call-out boxes (Professor Owl) that flag common mistakes, offer shortcuts, or pause on especially important insights. Reading a chapter in this order, objectives, content with examples, key terms, then practice problems, is the intended path through the material. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: How much time should I expect to spend on this course each week?
docs.text: While exact workload varies by student background and how the course is scheduled in a given term, a 16-chapter introductory economics textbook of this depth is typically paired with roughly 2 to 3 hours of reading and practice-problem work per chapter beyond any scheduled class time, which adds up to a few hours weekly outside of lecture during a normal semester pace of one chapter every week or two. Chapters with heavier quantitative content, such as Elasticity, Production and Costs, and Game Theory, generally take longer to work through carefully than more conceptual chapters like the introduction or behavioral economics, mainly because of the practice problems and graph work involved. Because later chapters build directly on earlier ones, spending adequate time on the foundational chapters (1 through 5) pays off by making the market-structure unit (Chapters 6 through 10) much faster to absorb. Using the MicroSims actively, rather than skimming past them, tends to shorten total study time because manipulating a model builds intuition faster than rereading static text. Ultimately, your own pace should be driven by whether you can complete the end-of-chapter practice problems correctly, not by a fixed clock target. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: How are the practice problems in each chapter meant to be used?
docs.text: The practice problems at the end of each chapter are designed as a self-check, not as graded homework by default: each one comes with a worked solution so you can verify your reasoning immediately rather than wondering whether you got it right. The most effective way to use them is to attempt each problem fully on your own first, including redrawing any graph from scratch, before looking at the solution, since the act of constructing the answer is what builds durable understanding. If your answer differs from the solution, trace back through your steps to find exactly where the reasoning diverged rather than simply re-reading the correct answer and moving on. For example, if you get the wrong equilibrium price in a supply-and-demand problem, check first whether you set up the two equations correctly, then whether your algebra solving them was correct, rather than assuming you simply don't understand equilibrium. Many chapters' problems are also spiraled: later practice problems quietly reuse skills from earlier chapters (an oligopoly problem might require marginal cost reasoning from Chapter 5), so working through problems chapter by chapter, in order, keeps those skills fresh for when they resurface. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: How do the six units of the course build on each other?
docs.text: The six units are sequenced so each one supplies tools the next unit needs. Unit 1 (Foundations) introduces scarcity, opportunity cost, marginal analysis, and the supply-and-demand framework that every later unit assumes you already know. Unit 2 (Consumer and Producer Theory) goes underneath that framework, explaining why demand curves and supply curves look the way they do by modeling individual consumer utility maximization and firm cost structures. Unit 3 (Market Structures) then asks: given those consumer and firm foundations, what happens when markets differ in how many sellers there are and how much power each one has, moving from perfect competition through monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, and finally formal game theory to handle strategic firms. Unit 4 (Factor Markets) takes the same marginal-revenue and marginal-cost logic from Unit 3 and applies it to how firms hire labor and capital rather than how they sell output. Unit 5 (Market Failures and Policy) shows what goes wrong when the efficient-market assumptions from Units 2 and 3 break down, covering externalities, public goods, and information problems, and what policies can fix each one. Unit 6 (Frontiers) revisits earlier assumptions, questioning whether consumers are as rational as Unit 2 assumed, and extends the market framework to international trade. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What should I do if I get stuck on a concept in the textbook?
docs.text: First, re-read the relevant section slowly and work through any worked example in it by hand, covering the solution and attempting it yourself before checking. Because this book is cumulative, confusion in a later chapter is very often rooted in a shaky grasp of an earlier concept, so if Chapter 7 on monopoly feels confusing, it is worth briefly revisiting marginal revenue and marginal cost in Chapter 6 rather than pushing forward. Second, actively use the interactive MicroSim for that concept if one is present in the section; manipulating the model yourself often resolves confusion that re-reading text cannot, because it lets you see cause and effect directly. Third, check the glossary entry for any term that feels unclear, since the book's glossary gives a precise, standalone definition (often with a concrete example) that may be phrased more simply than the in-chapter explanation. Fourth, attempt the end-of-chapter practice problems even if you are not fully confident, since working through a problem and then comparing it to the worked solution often clarifies a concept faster than passive re-reading. Finally, bring specific questions to office hours or discussion sections rather than a vague "I don't get this chapter," since identifying exactly which step confused you makes it much easier to get unstuck. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What will I be able to do by the end of this course that I can't do now?
docs.text: By the end of ECON 1101 you will be able to analyze real economic decisions and policy debates using a shared, rigorous toolkit rather than intuition alone. Concretely, you will be able to define core concepts like opportunity cost, marginal utility, price elasticity, and Nash equilibrium; explain how shifts in supply or demand move market equilibrium; and describe how perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly each determine price and output differently. You will be able to apply marginal analysis and supply-and-demand models to everyday and business decisions, including the effects of taxes, subsidies, and price controls, and apply game-theoretic reasoning to predict outcomes in competitive strategic settings such as pricing wars. You will be able to analyze how market structure and elasticity affect social welfare and the burden of a tax, and evaluate policy trade-offs such as tariffs versus free trade or a Pigouvian tax versus cap-and-trade using efficiency and equity criteria. Finally, you will be able to design and justify an original policy proposal addressing a specific market failure, such as a negative externality or a public good problem, using supply-and-demand and welfare analysis to support your recommendation. For example, you could evaluate whether a city should use a carbon tax or a cap-and-trade system to cut emissions and defend your choice with the course's own tools. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What is scarcity, and why is it considered the starting point of economics?
docs.text: Scarcity is the condition in which human wants for goods and services exceed the limited resources available to satisfy them, forcing choices about how those resources are used. It is the single fact that makes economics necessary at all: if resources were unlimited, there would be no need to choose, no prices, and no economic analysis required. Scarcity applies to individuals (a student has a limited number of hours in a day), firms (a factory has a limited amount of machinery and labor), and entire societies (a country has a limited amount of land, workers, and capital). For example, a country has enough resources to produce only a limited combination of food and clothing, so producing more of one usually requires producing less of the other, which is exactly what the Production Possibilities Frontier in Chapter 1 illustrates visually. Scarcity is distinct from poverty: even a wealthy society faces scarcity, because no society has literally unlimited resources relative to everyone's wants, even if its absolute level of resources is high. Nearly every concept that follows in this course, choice, opportunity cost, marginal analysis, supply and demand, is ultimately a tool for understanding how individuals and societies respond to scarcity. Glossary. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What is the difference between choice and opportunity cost?
docs.text: Choice is simply the decision to use a limited resource, such as time or money, for one purpose instead of another available purpose; it is the act of selecting among alternatives. Opportunity cost is what that choice costs you: specifically, the value of the next-best alternative you give up by making it. Every choice has an opportunity cost, but the two concepts answer different questions. "Choice" answers "what did you pick?" while "opportunity cost" answers "what did picking it cost you in terms of the next-best thing you gave up?" For example, choosing to spend $20 on a movie ticket is the choice; the opportunity cost of that choice is whatever else you valued most that $20 could have bought, such as a book you didn't buy. Opportunity costs are often hidden because they rarely appear on a receipt: the true opportunity cost of attending college includes not just tuition, but the wages you forwent by not working full time instead. Economists emphasize opportunity cost because comparing only the dollar price of options, while ignoring what else was given up, leads to systematically poor decisions. Recognizing both concepts together, and distinguishing a choice from its cost, is the foundation for every later tool in the course, especially marginal analysis. Glossary. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What does the law of demand say, and why does it usually hold?
docs.text: The law of demand states that, holding other factors constant, the quantity demanded of a good falls as its price rises, and rises as its price falls. In other words, demand curves slope downward. This usually holds for two related reasons. First, the substitution effect: as a good becomes relatively more expensive, buyers switch toward cheaper substitutes that satisfy a similar need. Second, the income effect: a higher price reduces a buyer's effective purchasing power, leading them to buy less of many goods, including this one, in most cases. For example, when the price of movie tickets rises, some moviegoers switch to streaming at home (substitution), and others simply attend fewer movies overall because their budget feels tighter (income effect). The law of demand is considered one of the most reliable empirical regularities in economics, holding across an enormous range of goods and markets, though a theoretical exception exists for Giffen goods, where a strong negative income effect for a very important inferior good can outweigh the substitution effect. Understanding why the law of demand holds, rather than simply memorizing that demand curves slope downward, is what allows you to correctly predict what happens when income, not price, changes instead. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What distinguishes a firm's short run from its long run?
docs.text: The short run is a time period in which a firm can adjust some inputs, such as how many workers it hires or how many hours it operates, but at least one input, typically plant size or heavy capital equipment, is fixed and cannot be changed. The long run is a time period long enough that the firm can adjust all of its inputs, including fixed ones like plant size, and can even enter or exit the industry entirely. The distinction is not about a fixed amount of calendar time; it depends on the specific input and industry. For a small bakery, "long run" might mean a few months, since leasing a bigger oven is relatively quick; for a semiconductor fabrication plant, the long run might span several years, since building new capacity takes that long. This distinction matters because a firm's cost structure, and therefore its optimal decisions, look different in each period. In the short run, fixed costs must be paid no matter what, which is why the shutdown rule in Chapter 6 only compares price to average variable cost. In the long run, every cost becomes effectively variable, because the firm could in principle avoid it entirely by exiting, which is why long-run equilibrium in perfect competition drives economic profit to zero. Glossary. Chapter 5: Production and Costs

docs.title: What is market failure, and what are its main categories?
docs.text: Market failure is a situation in which a market, left on its own, fails to allocate resources efficiently, meaning it does not produce the quantity of a good or service that maximizes total social welfare. The course covers three broad categories. The first is externalities, costs or benefits of an activity that fall on third parties not involved in the transaction, such as pollution from a factory harming nearby residents who had no say in the decision. The second is problems with public goods and common-pool resources, which arise because some goods are hard to exclude non-payers from (leading to free-riding) or because shared resources get overused when no one owns them (the tragedy of the commons). The third is information problems, including asymmetric information that leads to adverse selection and moral hazard, where one side of a transaction knows something important that the other side does not. Market power itself, such as that held by a monopoly, is also classified as a form of market failure because it restricts output below the efficient level. For example, a factory that pollutes a river without paying for the damage is a classic market failure, since its private costs don't reflect the true social cost of its production. Glossary. Chapter 12: Market Failures

docs.title: What is marginal analysis, and why do economists say to think "at the margin"?
docs.text: Marginal analysis is a method of decision-making that compares the additional benefit of one more unit of an action to its additional cost, rather than comparing only total benefits to total costs. The core decision rule is to keep doing an activity as long as its marginal benefit is at least as large as its marginal cost, and to stop once marginal cost would exceed marginal benefit. Economists emphasize thinking "at the margin" because most real decisions are not all-or-nothing; they are about whether to do a little bit more or a little bit less of something you are already doing. For example, a firm deciding whether to produce one more unit of output should not ask whether production overall is profitable, but whether that specific next unit's revenue exceeds its specific additional cost. Marginal analysis explains behavior that would look puzzling if you only considered totals: a restaurant might keep seating one more table even on a slow night, because the marginal cost of that table (a bit more food and labor) is lower than the marginal revenue it brings in, even if the restaurant's total profit for the night is low. This single idea, comparing marginal benefit to marginal cost, reappears in nearly every later chapter, from a consumer's last dollar of spending to a monopolist's last unit of output. Glossary. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What is a market, and what conditions does it need to function well?
docs.text: A market is an arrangement, physical or virtual, through which buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods, services, or resources. A farmers market, a stock exchange, and a ride-sharing app are all markets, even though they look very different, because each one connects people who want to buy with people who want to sell. For a market to allocate resources efficiently, it generally needs clear information about prices and product quality, enough buyers and sellers that no single participant can dictate the price, the ability for buyers and sellers to freely enter or exit, and property rights clear enough that trades can actually be enforced. When these conditions hold reasonably well, as they do in markets for many agricultural commodities, the price system does a remarkably good job of coordinating the decisions of thousands of independent buyers and sellers without any central planner. When one of these conditions breaks down significantly, for instance when one seller dominates the market (monopoly) or when buyers cannot verify product quality (information asymmetry), the market can fail to produce an efficient outcome, which is exactly the subject of the market-structure and market-failure units later in the course. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What is demand, and how is it different from quantity demanded?
docs.text: Demand is the entire relationship describing the willingness and ability of buyers to purchase different quantities of a good at every possible price during a given time period; it is represented visually by the whole demand curve. Quantity demanded, by contrast, is a single number: the specific amount buyers want to purchase at one particular price. The distinction matters because it tells you which direction causation runs on a graph. A change in the good's own price moves you along a fixed demand curve, changing the quantity demanded, but it does not shift the curve itself. A change in anything else that affects buying behavior, such as income, tastes, the price of a related good, or buyer expectations, shifts the entire demand curve to a new position, which economists call a change in demand. For example, if the price of coffee falls and people buy more cups, that is an increase in quantity demanded, a movement along the existing demand curve. But if a health report convinces people coffee is good for them and they buy more cups at every price level, that is an increase in demand, a shift of the whole curve to the right. Keeping this distinction straight is essential for correctly reading every supply-and-demand graph in the course. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What is a demand curve, and what causes it to shift versus simply move along it?
docs.text: A demand curve is a graph showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity of it that buyers wish to purchase, holding all other factors constant; it typically slopes downward, consistent with the law of demand. A movement along a fixed demand curve happens only when the good's own price changes, nothing else, and it changes quantity demanded without relocating the curve. A shift of the entire curve happens when one of the determinants of demand changes instead, for example a change in consumer income, tastes, the price of a substitute or complement good, buyer expectations about the future, or the number of buyers in the market. An increase in income raising demand for a normal good, or a lower price of a complementary good like coffee creamer raising demand for coffee, are both shifts, moving the whole curve rightward. Confusing a shift with a movement is one of the most common errors students make when first learning supply and demand, so it is worth double-checking, whenever a problem changes something, whether that something is the good's own price (movement) or a different variable entirely (shift). Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What is supply, and what does the law of supply say about sellers' behavior?
docs.text: Supply is the willingness and ability of sellers to offer different quantities of a good for sale at different prices during a given time period, represented by the entire supply curve. The law of supply states that, holding other factors constant, the quantity supplied of a good rises as its price rises, and falls as its price falls, which is why supply curves typically slope upward. This pattern makes economic sense because higher prices make production more profitable at the margin, encouraging existing sellers to produce more and sometimes drawing new sellers into the market, while sellers facing rising marginal costs as they expand output need a higher price to justify producing additional units. For example, a wheat farmer's supply describes how many bushels he is willing to sell at $5 per bushel versus $8 per bushel, with higher prices generally inducing more bushels offered, partly because it becomes worth using less ideal land or paying overtime wages to harvest more. Just like demand, supply has determinants other than price, such as input costs, technology, and the number of sellers, and a change in one of these shifts the entire supply curve rather than simply moving along it. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What are consumer surplus and producer surplus, and how do they combine into total surplus?
docs.text: Consumer surplus is the difference between the maximum price a buyer is willing to pay for a good and the price they actually pay, summed across all buyers in a market; it measures the net benefit buyers receive from being able to trade. Producer surplus is the mirror image: the difference between the price a seller actually receives and the minimum price at which they would have been willing to sell, summed across all sellers; it measures sellers' net benefit from trading. Total surplus is simply consumer surplus plus producer surplus, and it is the standard measure economists use for the overall gains from trade that a market generates. For example, if a buyer would have paid up to $10 for a shirt but pays only $7, she gains $3 of consumer surplus; if the seller would have accepted as little as $4 but receives $7, he gains $3 of producer surplus, for $6 of total surplus from that single transaction. A perfectly competitive market in equilibrium maximizes total surplus, which is exactly why economists treat deviations from that equilibrium, caused by taxes, price controls, or market power, as sources of lost efficiency, or deadweight loss. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What is the production function, and how does it connect to a firm's costs?
docs.text: A production function is a relationship showing the maximum quantity of output a firm can produce from given quantities of inputs, such as labor and capital, using current technology. For example, a production function might show that a bakery using 5 workers and 2 ovens can produce at most 300 loaves of bread per day; using more workers or ovens would allow more output, up to the limits of the function. The production function is the physical, engineering-like foundation underneath a firm's cost curves: once you know how much output a given combination of inputs can produce, and you know the price of each input, you can translate that physical relationship directly into a cost relationship. If labor eventually experiences diminishing marginal returns, meaning each additional worker adds less extra output than the one before, holding capital fixed, then the firm's short-run marginal cost curve will eventually rise as output increases, because each additional unit of output requires relatively more of the increasingly less productive input. This connection between the production function and cost curves is why Chapter 5 introduces the production function first: understanding what a firm can physically produce from its inputs is the key to understanding why its costs behave the way they do, which in turn drives every market-structure model in the chapters that follow. Glossary. Chapter 5: Production and Costs

docs.title: What are the defining features of perfect competition?
docs.text: Perfect competition is a market structure characterized by four conditions: many small buyers and sellers, so no single participant can influence the market price; identical (homogeneous) products, so buyers have no reason to prefer one seller's good over another's; free entry and exit, so firms can start up or leave the industry without significant barriers; and full information, so buyers and sellers know prices and product quality. Together, these conditions make every firm a price taker, meaning it has no ability to set its own price and must simply accept whatever the market determines. Markets for many agricultural commodities, such as wheat, closely approximate perfect competition, since no single farmer's decision to produce more or less noticeably moves the market price. Perfect competition is important less because it describes every real market perfectly, and more because it serves as the efficiency benchmark against which every other market structure in the course, monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly, is compared. In long-run competitive equilibrium, firms earn zero economic profit and price equals the minimum long-run average cost, which is also exactly the condition for allocative efficiency: price equals marginal cost, so total surplus is maximized. Glossary. Chapter 6: Perfect Competition

docs.title: What gives a monopoly its market power, and how does that change its pricing decision compared to a competitive firm?
docs.text: A monopoly is a market structure in which a single firm is the only seller of a good or service that has no close substitutes, and its market power comes from a barrier to entry that keeps rival firms out, such as a patent, control of an essential input, government licensing, or, in the case of a natural monopoly, cost conditions that make it cheapest for only one firm to serve the whole market. Because a monopolist faces the entire downward-sloping market demand curve rather than a flat, price-taking demand curve, it becomes a price maker: it can influence price by choosing how much output to produce. This changes its marginal revenue: selling one more unit requires lowering the price on all units sold, not just the extra one, so a monopolist's marginal revenue is always below its price, unlike a competitive firm whose marginal revenue equals price. The monopolist still follows the same MR = MC rule to find its profit-maximizing quantity, but then charges whatever price the demand curve indicates buyers will pay for that quantity, a price that exceeds marginal cost. For example, a local water utility that is the only provider of piped water to a city can set a price well above its marginal cost of delivering more water, something a competitive wheat farmer could never do. Glossary. Chapter 7: Monopoly

docs.title: What is monopolistic competition, and how does it differ from both perfect competition and monopoly?
docs.text: Monopolistic competition is a market structure with many sellers offering similar but not identical products, free entry and exit, and each firm having some control over its own price because of product differentiation. It borrows features from both ends of the market-structure spectrum: like perfect competition, it has many firms and free entry and exit, which drives economic profit to zero in the long run; but like monopoly, each firm has some pricing power because its product is not perfectly identical to its rivals' products, giving it a small downward-sloping demand curve rather than a perfectly flat one. For example, restaurants in a city compete under monopolistic competition, since each offers a somewhat different dining experience but faces many competing establishments offering similar, substitutable meals. The key long-run outcome that distinguishes it from perfect competition is excess capacity: because each firm's demand curve is still downward-sloping rather than flat, long-run equilibrium occurs where price equals average total cost, but not at the minimum point of that average-cost curve, leaving firms operating below their most efficient scale even though they earn zero economic profit. This trade-off, slightly higher costs in exchange for the genuine product variety consumers value, is central to evaluating whether monopolistic competition is "good" or "bad" for consumers. Glossary. Chapter 8: Monopolistic Competition

docs.title: How is market equilibrium determined, and what happens if price starts above or below it?
docs.text: Market equilibrium is the price and quantity at which the quantity buyers wish to purchase exactly equals the quantity sellers wish to offer, found graphically where the demand curve and supply curve intersect; at that point, there is no economic pressure for price to change. If price starts above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a market surplus (unsold goods piling up), which pressures sellers to cut prices to clear their inventory, moving price back down toward equilibrium. If price starts below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a market shortage, which lets sellers raise prices without losing many sales, since eager buyers will pay more rather than go without, moving price back up toward equilibrium. For example, if a popular concert sets ticket prices too low, demand outstrips the available seats, creating a shortage that in an unregulated market would push the price upward until it clears. This self-correcting tendency is why markets tend to settle at equilibrium even without anyone deliberately aiming for it: it is simply the only price where neither buyers' nor sellers' behavior creates further pressure for change. Government price controls, like a price ceiling or floor, work by deliberately preventing the market from reaching this natural equilibrium. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: How do I apply the laws of demand and supply to predict what happens to equilibrium price and quantity when demand or supply shifts?
docs.text: The standard method is to shift one curve at a time, redraw the graph, and read the new intersection. If demand increases (the curve shifts right), both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity rise, because at the old price there is now excess demand pulling price up, and the higher price draws out more quantity supplied along the existing supply curve. If demand decreases (shifts left), both equilibrium price and quantity fall. If supply increases (the curve shifts right), equilibrium price falls while equilibrium quantity rises, since more is being offered at every price, and buyers are drawn to buy more only once the price moves down. If supply decreases (shifts left), equilibrium price rises while equilibrium quantity falls. When both curves shift at the same time, you can determine the direction of the equilibrium quantity change if both shifts push it the same way, but the price change may be ambiguous without knowing the relative size of each shift, and vice versa for quantity. For example, a drought (supply decreases) combined with a health trend raising demand for a vegetable will unambiguously raise its equilibrium price, but the effect on quantity depends on which shift is larger. Practicing this one-curve-at-a-time method on many scenarios is the fastest way to build reliable intuition for supply-and-demand problems. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What is price elasticity of demand, and what does a specific numerical value tell you about buyer behavior?
docs.text: Price elasticity of demand measures how much the quantity demanded of a good changes in percentage terms in response to a one-percent change in its price; it is essentially a measure of how sensitive buyers are to price changes. A specific numerical value tells you the magnitude of that sensitivity: an elasticity of -2 means a 1% price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by about 2%, which economists call elastic demand (elasticity greater than 1 in absolute value), while an elasticity of -0.5 means the same 1% price increase causes only a 0.5% fall in quantity demanded, which is inelastic demand (less than 1 in absolute value). An elasticity of exactly -1 is unit-elastic. For example, demand for a specific brand of soda tends to be elastic because buyers can easily switch to another brand, while demand for insulin tends to be inelastic because patients who need it keep buying it even as price rises significantly. Knowing whether a good's demand is elastic or inelastic has immediate practical value: it tells a seller whether raising price will raise or lower total revenue, and it tells a policymaker who actually bears the burden of a tax placed on that good. Glossary. Chapter 3: Elasticity

docs.title: How do I use marginal analysis to decide how much of something to produce or consume?
docs.text: The method is always the same: identify the marginal benefit and marginal cost of one additional unit, and keep going as long as marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost, stopping exactly where they are equal (or where the next unit would make marginal cost exceed marginal benefit). For a consumer, this might mean comparing the extra satisfaction (marginal utility) from one more slice of pizza to its price; for a firm, it means comparing the extra revenue from producing one more unit (marginal revenue) to the extra cost of producing it (marginal cost). The key discipline is to ignore totals and ignore sunk costs, focusing only on the next increment. For example, a firm should not ask "is this product line profitable overall?" when deciding whether to produce one more unit; it should ask "does the revenue from this specific next unit exceed the cost of making it?" Even a firm with large total losses should keep producing additional units as long as each one individually adds more revenue than cost, since refusing to produce a worthwhile marginal unit only makes the total loss larger. This marginal, unit-by-unit logic is the single most reused decision rule in the entire course. Glossary. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: How do I use the MR = MC rule to find a profit-maximizing firm's output level?
docs.text: The MR = MC rule states that a firm maximizes profit by producing the quantity of output at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost; producing less than this quantity leaves profitable units unproduced, while producing more than this quantity means the last units cost more to make than they bring in. To apply it, write down or sketch the firm's marginal revenue curve and marginal cost curve as functions of quantity, then find the output level where they cross. For a price-taking competitive firm, marginal revenue is simply the constant market price, so the rule simplifies to producing where price equals marginal cost. For a firm with market power, like a monopolist, marginal revenue is below price and declining, so you must find marginal revenue specifically (not just use the price) before setting it equal to marginal cost. For example, if a firm's marginal cost of the 100th unit is $8 and its marginal revenue from that unit is $10, it should produce that unit, since it adds $2 to profit; but if the 101st unit's marginal cost rises to $11 while marginal revenue stays near $10, the firm should stop at 100 units. This same rule, with the details of marginal revenue changing by market structure, appears again in every market-structure chapter. Glossary. Chapter 6: Perfect Competition

docs.title: What is the production possibilities frontier (PPF), and how do I use it to show opportunity cost and the gains from specialization?
docs.text: The production possibilities frontier is a curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy (or a firm, or a person) can produce given its fixed resources and current technology; for example, a frontier might show an economy can produce 100 cars and 0 computers, 0 cars and 200 computers, or any combination of the two along the curve between them. Any point on the frontier represents full, efficient use of resources, any point inside it represents waste or unemployment of resources, and any point outside it is currently unattainable. You use the PPF to show opportunity cost by comparing two points on the curve: moving from one point to another and giving up some units of one good to gain units of the other reveals the opportunity cost of that trade-off directly, and the PPF is typically bowed outward because of increasing opportunity cost, since resources are not equally well suited to every use. You use it to show the gains from specialization and trade by comparing two separate producers' individual frontiers to a combined frontier: if each producer specializes in the good for which they have a comparative advantage (the lower opportunity cost) and then trades, the two together can consume combinations of goods that lie outside what either frontier alone could produce. Glossary. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What is consumer optimum, and how does a consumer use marginal reasoning to decide what bundle of goods to buy?
docs.text: Consumer optimum is the combination of goods a consumer chooses that maximizes total satisfaction (utility) given the limits of their budget constraint; for example, a consumer's optimum might be 4 apples and 3 oranges, the affordable bundle that leaves her as satisfied as possible among everything she could afford. The marginal reasoning behind finding it is the equal marginal principle: a consumer with a limited budget maximizes total utility by allocating spending so that the marginal utility per dollar spent is equal across every good purchased. If a dollar spent on apples currently buys more extra satisfaction than a dollar spent on oranges, the consumer is not yet at the optimum and should shift spending toward apples; she keeps reallocating until an additional dollar would yield the same extra satisfaction no matter which good it was spent on. For example, a consumer stops buying more apples and starts buying oranges once a dollar spent on oranges yields as much extra satisfaction as a dollar spent on apples. This same logic, formalized graphically using indifference curves and a budget line, is what Chapter 4 calls the tangency condition, where the consumer's optimum occurs where the budget line is just tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve. Glossary. Chapter 4: Consumer Theory

docs.title: How do economies of scale shape a firm's long-run average cost curve, and what does that mean for how big a firm should grow?
docs.text: Economies of scale occur when a firm's long-run average cost falls as it increases the scale of its output, often because fixed costs like expensive machinery get spread over more units, or because larger scale allows specialization and bulk purchasing discounts. For example, a car manufacturer that spreads the cost of expensive machinery over a much larger number of vehicles experiences economies of scale, lowering its average cost per car as volume rises. Diseconomies of scale occur at the opposite extreme: long-run average cost rises as output grows further, often due to coordination and management difficulties within a very large organization, such as added layers of management slowing decisions and raising costs per unit. Together these two forces give the long-run average cost curve its typical U-shape, falling at first due to economies of scale and eventually rising due to diseconomies of scale, with the minimum point called the minimum efficient scale, the smallest output level at which the firm achieves its lowest possible average cost. For a firm deciding how big to grow, this curve indicates the output range where it is operating most cost-efficiently; growing well past the minimum efficient scale into the diseconomies-of-scale region raises average cost and can leave the firm less able to compete on price. Glossary. Chapter 5: Production and Costs

docs.title: Why does deadweight loss arise when a market produces something other than the efficient quantity, and how does this connect the efficiency of perfect competition to the inefficiency of monopoly?
docs.text: Deadweight loss is the loss of total surplus to society that occurs when a market produces less (or more) than the efficient quantity, the quantity at which price equals marginal cost. It arises because, at any quantity below the efficient level, there exist potential trades between buyers and sellers, a buyer willing to pay more than it would cost the seller to produce, that simply never happen, destroying the surplus those trades would have created. In long-run competitive equilibrium under perfect competition, free entry and exit and price-taking behavior push price down to equal marginal cost exactly, so no such mutually beneficial trade is left unmade, and total surplus is maximized with zero deadweight loss, this is allocative efficiency. A monopolist, by contrast, deliberately restricts output below this efficient quantity in order to raise price and maximize its own profit, since it sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost rather than price equal to marginal cost, and marginal revenue lies below price for a firm with market power. The resulting gap between the competitive outcome and the monopoly outcome, is exactly the monopoly's deadweight loss: the trades between willing buyers and the firm's low-cost production capacity that never happen because the monopolist found it more profitable to restrict output and charge more. Glossary. Chapter 7: Monopoly

docs.title: How are the different types of market failure, externalities, public goods, market power, and information problems, related to each other?
docs.text: All of these market failures share a common root: in each case, the price a decision-maker faces fails to reflect the true social cost or benefit of their choice, so the market's otherwise reliable "invisible hand" steers resources to an inefficient outcome. With externalities, a third party bears a cost or enjoys a benefit that never shows up in the price the buyer and seller negotiate, so the private market price understates the true social cost (negative externalities) or benefit (positive externalities) of the activity. With public goods, the problem is that non-excludability lets people free-ride, consuming the good without paying for it, so no individual seller can charge a price that reflects the good's full social value, leading to underprovision relative to what society would actually want. With market power, as in monopoly, the firm deliberately restricts output to raise price above marginal cost, meaning the price again fails to reflect the true marginal cost of production. With information problems like adverse selection and moral hazard, one side of a transaction cannot accurately observe quality or behavior, so the price charged reflects an average that misprices individual, differently-informed participants. In every case, the common fix is a policy tool, taxes, subsidies, regulation, or better information design, that realigns the price signal with the true social cost or benefit. Glossary. Chapter 12: Market Failures

docs.title: What is oligopoly, and why does strategic interdependence make it harder to analyze than perfect competition or monopoly?
docs.text: Oligopoly is a market structure dominated by a small number of large firms whose decisions about price and output significantly affect one another; the commercial airplane manufacturing industry, dominated by just a couple of major producers, is a real-world example. What makes oligopoly fundamentally different, and harder to analyze, from perfect competition and monopoly is strategic interdependence: the condition in which each firm's best choice of price or output depends directly on the choices made by its rivals. A perfectly competitive firm can ignore its competitors entirely, since no single firm's output decision moves the market price; a monopolist faces no rivals at all, only the overall market demand curve. An oligopolist, by contrast, must explicitly predict and react to what its rivals will do, since a price cut or output increase by one firm changes the profitable choice for every other firm in the market. This is precisely why oligopoly cannot be solved with the simple price-taking or single-firm-demand tools used in earlier chapters, and why the course introduces formal game theory, dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium, and backward induction immediately after the oligopoly chapter, as the dedicated toolkit for reasoning through this kind of mutual, interdependent decision-making. Glossary. Chapter 9: Oligopoly

docs.title: What is the formal definition of opportunity cost, and how is it different from a sunk cost?
docs.text: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when a person or society chooses one option over another; it is always forward-looking, describing what you are giving up by making a choice right now. A sunk cost is a cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, and it is always backward-looking, describing money or effort already spent in the past. The crucial technical distinction is that rational decision-making should always account fully for opportunity costs but should always ignore sunk costs, because a sunk cost does not change regardless of what you decide to do next, while an opportunity cost does change depending on what alternative you choose. For example, money already spent on a non-refundable concert ticket is a sunk cost and should not influence whether you attend if a better opportunity arises, since that money is gone either way; but the opportunity cost of attending the concert anyway, namely the value of whatever else you could have done with that evening, is very much relevant to the decision. Students often conflate the two, reasoning "I already paid for this, so I should use it," which is exactly the sunk cost fallacy this course warns against from Chapter 1 onward. Glossary. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: What is the difference between a normal good and an inferior good?
docs.text: A normal good is a good for which quantity demanded rises when buyer income rises, and falls when income falls, holding price constant; restaurant dining is a normal good for most people, since they eat out more often as their income increases. An inferior good is the opposite: quantity demanded falls when income rises, and rises when income falls, holding price constant; instant noodles may be an inferior good if people buy less of them once they can afford pricier meals as their income grows. The label "inferior" describes the good's relationship to income, not its physical quality; an inferior good can be perfectly fine, it is simply something people buy less of as they become able to afford better alternatives. This classification is formalized by income elasticity of demand: a positive income elasticity identifies a normal good, while a negative income elasticity identifies an inferior good. Both classifications are determined empirically by observing how quantity demanded actually responds to income changes for a specific good and a specific population, which means the same good could in principle be a normal good for one group of buyers and an inferior good for another, depending on their circumstances and preferences. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What are substitute goods and complement goods, and how can you tell them apart?
docs.text: Substitute goods are two goods for which an increase in the price of one causes an increase in demand for the other, because buyers can use either one to satisfy a similar need; butter and margarine are substitute goods, since a higher price of butter tends to increase demand for margarine as buyers switch toward it. Complement goods are two goods for which an increase in the price of one causes a decrease in demand for the other, because the two goods are typically used together; coffee and coffee creamer are complements, so a higher price of coffee tends to decrease demand for creamer, since people buy less coffee overall. The technical way to tell them apart is the sign of their cross-price elasticity of demand: a positive cross-price elasticity (quantity demanded of good A rises when the price of good B rises) identifies substitutes, while a negative cross-price elasticity identifies complements. In practice, you can usually tell which relationship applies to two particular goods by asking whether they are typically used as alternatives to each other (substitutes) or used together in the same activity (complements), though the cross-price elasticity calculation gives the precise, data-based answer when the intuitive classification is ambiguous. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What is the difference between fixed cost and variable cost?
docs.text: Fixed cost is a cost of production that does not change with the quantity of output produced in the short run; a factory's rent payment is a fixed cost because it must be paid whether the factory produces 100 units or zero units that month. Variable cost is a cost of production that does change with the quantity of output produced; the cost of raw materials used in manufacturing rises and falls with the number of units a factory produces, making it a variable cost. The distinction is specifically a short-run concept: in the long run, a firm can adjust every input, including ones that were fixed in the short run (like plant size), which is why economists say there are no truly fixed costs in the long run. This distinction matters directly for a firm's shutdown decision: because fixed costs must be paid regardless of output level, a firm comparing whether to produce at all in the short run should ignore fixed costs and compare price only to average variable cost, since fixed costs are unavoidable either way and therefore irrelevant at the margin, in the same spirit as ignoring a sunk cost. Glossary. Chapter 5: Production and Costs

docs.title: What is a price taker versus a price maker?
docs.text: A price taker is a buyer or seller in a market who has no ability to influence the market price and must simply accept the price determined by the overall market; a wheat farmer selling into a large competitive market is a price taker, since his individual decision to sell more or less has no noticeable effect on the going market price. A price maker is a seller with enough market power to influence the price of its product by changing the quantity it offers for sale, rather than simply accepting a price handed to it by the market; a monopolist is the clearest example, since it is the only seller and therefore directly determines the trade-off between quantity sold and the price charged. The technical difference shows up in each firm's marginal revenue: a price taker's marginal revenue equals the fixed market price for every unit sold, giving it a perfectly flat (horizontal) demand curve from its own point of view, while a price maker's marginal revenue lies below price and falls as output rises, because selling one more unit requires lowering the price on every unit sold, not just the additional one. Whether a firm is a price taker or price maker is the single most important fact determining which market-structure model (perfect competition versus monopoly, monopolistic competition, or oligopoly) applies to it. Glossary. Chapter 6: Perfect Competition

docs.title: What are the four classic market structures, and what feature mainly distinguishes them?
docs.text: The four classic market structures covered in this course are perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly. The feature that mainly distinguishes them is the number of sellers combined with how differentiated their products are and how much individual pricing power each firm has as a result. Perfect competition has many sellers with an identical product and no pricing power (pure price takers). Monopoly has a single seller with no close substitutes and full pricing power (a pure price maker). Monopolistic competition has many sellers like perfect competition, but each sells a somewhat differentiated product, giving each firm a small amount of pricing power. Oligopoly has only a small number of large sellers, who may sell identical or differentiated products, but whose decisions are strategically interdependent, meaning each firm's choices directly affect, and are affected by, its rivals' choices in a way that does not occur in the other three structures. Economists also use measures like the concentration ratio and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index to classify real industries into one of these four categories based on how concentrated market share is among the top firms. Glossary. Chapter 6: Perfect Competition

docs.title: What's the difference between economic profit and accounting profit?
docs.text: Accounting profit is the difference between a firm's total revenue and its explicit costs only, meaning costs that involve an actual cash payment, such as wages, rent, and materials; it is the profit figure that would appear on a conventional accounting statement. Economic profit is the difference between total revenue and total costs, including both those same explicit costs and the implicit opportunity cost of resources the owner supplies themselves, such as the wages they gave up by not working elsewhere or the return they gave up by investing their own capital in this business instead of another one. For example, a business owner earning $50,000 in accounting profit but who gave up a $60,000 salaried job to run the business actually has an economic loss of $10,000, even though the accounting books show a positive profit. This difference matters because economists use economic profit, not accounting profit, to determine whether a firm should actually stay in an industry: zero economic profit means the firm is earning exactly enough to cover every cost, including opportunity costs, which is precisely the condition that defines long-run competitive equilibrium, even though the firm's accounting profit in that state is typically positive. Glossary. Chapter 6: Perfect Competition

docs.title: What's the difference between marginal cost and average total cost, and why can one be rising while the other is falling?
docs.text: Marginal cost is the additional cost incurred from producing one more unit of output; average total cost is total cost divided by the quantity of output produced, essentially the cost per unit averaged across everything made so far. They can move in opposite directions at the same output level because of a basic mathematical relationship: whenever marginal cost is below average total cost, producing one more unit pulls the average down, so average total cost is falling; whenever marginal cost is above average total cost, the next unit pulls the average up, so average total cost is rising. This is exactly why the marginal cost curve crosses the average total cost curve precisely at the average total cost curve's minimum point: marginal cost is below average cost (pulling it down) up to that point, and above average cost (pulling it up) after it. For example, if a firm's average total cost is $10 per unit but the next unit costs only $7 to produce, making that unit lowers the average to somewhere between $7 and $10, even though the firm's total cost has risen. Understanding this relationship is essential for correctly reading any cost-curve diagram in Chapters 5 and 6. Glossary. Chapter 5: Production and Costs

docs.title: What's the difference between allocative efficiency and productive efficiency?
docs.text: Productive efficiency is a situation in which goods are produced using the fewest possible resources, so no more of one good can be produced without producing less of another; it corresponds to operating exactly on the production possibilities frontier rather than inside it, and for a firm it typically means producing at the minimum point of its average total cost curve. Allocative efficiency is a stronger, different condition: resources are allocated so that producing one more unit of a good provides a benefit to society exactly equal to its cost, meaning price equals marginal cost. A market can be productively efficient (each firm minimizes its own cost per unit) without being allocatively efficient (the market as a whole still produces too little or too much relative to what society actually values). Perfectly competitive markets achieve both in long-run equilibrium, since free entry and exit drives firms to their minimum average cost (productive efficiency) at the same quantity where price equals marginal cost (allocative efficiency). A monopoly, by contrast, typically fails to achieve allocative efficiency, because it deliberately restricts output and prices above marginal cost, even if the firm itself is internally well-managed and minimizes its own production costs. Glossary. Chapter 6: Perfect Competition

docs.title: What's the difference between a change in demand and a change in quantity demanded?
docs.text: A change in quantity demanded refers only to a movement along a fixed, unchanged demand curve, caused exclusively by a change in the good's own price; nothing about the underlying relationship between price and buyer behavior has changed, only where on that existing relationship you currently are. A change in demand refers to the entire demand curve shifting to a new position on the graph, caused by a change in one of the determinants of demand other than the good's own price, such as income, tastes, the price of a related good, buyer expectations, or the number of buyers. For example, a rise in consumer income is a determinant of demand that can shift the entire demand curve for restaurant meals rightward (a change in demand), whereas a restaurant simply lowering its own prices and selling more meals as a result is only a movement along its existing demand curve (a change in quantity demanded). This exact distinction also applies on the supply side, between a change in supply (the curve shifts) and a change in quantity supplied (movement along a fixed curve caused only by the good's own price). Mixing these up is one of the most common mistakes on supply-and-demand exam problems. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: What's the difference between the income effect and the substitution effect?
docs.text: The substitution effect is the change in quantity demanded of a good that results from a change in its price relative to other goods, holding the consumer's overall satisfaction level constant; when the price of beef rises relative to chicken, consumers who buy more chicken instead of beef are responding to the substitution effect, since beef has become relatively more expensive regardless of their income. The income effect is the change in quantity demanded that results from a change in a consumer's purchasing power caused by the price change itself, holding relative prices constant; when the price of gasoline falls, a driver's effective purchasing power rises, and the resulting increase in driving distance partly reflects the income effect, separate from any substitution toward driving relative to other activities. Both effects normally push a demand curve in the same direction for a normal good, which is exactly why ordinary demand curves slope downward so reliably. The two effects can work against each other for an inferior good, and in the rare theoretical case of a Giffen good, a very strong negative income effect for an essential inferior good can actually outweigh the substitution effect, causing quantity demanded to fall as price falls, violating the usual law of demand. Glossary. Chapter 4: Consumer Theory

docs.title: What's the difference between adverse selection and moral hazard?
docs.text: Adverse selection is a problem arising from information asymmetry in which the party with less information ends up disproportionately attracting the riskiest or lowest-quality counterparts before a transaction occurs; an insurance company offering the same health insurance premium to everyone may attract mostly sicker applicants, since healthier people find the premium less worthwhile. Moral hazard is a different problem, also arising from information asymmetry, but it occurs after a transaction takes place: one party changes their behavior to take on more risk because the other party bears some of the consequences of that risk. A driver with full car insurance coverage might drive a little less carefully, knowing the insurance company will cover most of the cost of any accident, illustrating moral hazard. The key technical distinction is timing and mechanism: adverse selection is about who selects into a transaction based on hidden characteristics known before the deal is struck, while moral hazard is about how behavior changes after the deal is struck because incentives to be careful have been weakened. Both problems commonly coexist in the same market, such as health insurance, which is part of why insurance contracts often include deductibles and co-payments, designed to address moral hazard, alongside medical underwriting, designed to address adverse selection. Glossary. Chapter 14: Information Economics

docs.title: What's the difference between a negative externality and a positive externality?
docs.text: A negative externality is an externality in which a third party bears a cost from an economic activity, causing the market to produce more of the good than is socially efficient, because the price charged does not reflect the full social cost; air pollution from a power plant that harms the health of nearby residents who have no say in the plant's operation is a negative externality. A positive externality is the opposite: a third party receives a benefit from an economic activity, causing the market to produce less of the good than is socially efficient, because the price charged does not reflect the full social benefit; a beekeeper's bees pollinating a neighboring farmer's crops, boosting that farmer's harvest for free, is a positive externality. The policy implication is also opposite: a negative externality calls for a Pigouvian tax, set equal to the external cost per unit, to discourage overproduction, while a positive externality calls for a Pigouvian subsidy, set equal to the external benefit per unit, to encourage more of the socially beneficial activity. In both cases, the goal is the same: make the private decision-maker's incentives reflect the full social marginal cost or benefit of the activity, not just their own private cost or benefit. Glossary. Chapter 13: Externalities and Public Goods

docs.title: What's the difference between a public good and a common-pool resource?
docs.text: Both are classified using two properties: excludability, whether it is possible to prevent non-payers from consuming a good, and rivalry, whether one person's consumption reduces what is available to others. A public good is both non-excludable and non-rival, meaning it is difficult to prevent people from using it without paying, and one person's use does not reduce its availability to others; national defense is a public good because protecting the country does not prevent any individual citizen from also being protected, and non-payers cannot easily be excluded. A common-pool resource is non-excludable but rival, meaning it is still difficult to prevent access, but one person's use does reduce what remains for others; fish in an open ocean are a common-pool resource, since anyone can fish there, but each fish caught is no longer available to other fishers. Both share the free-riding problem that comes from non-excludability, but only the common-pool resource also suffers from the tragedy of the commons, overuse and depletion because individual users bear only part of the cost of their own use, which is why fisheries and shared pastures face a distinct overuse problem that national defense does not. Glossary. Chapter 13: Externalities and Public Goods

docs.title: How do you calculate average total cost, and what does it mean if it's higher than price?
docs.text: Average total cost is calculated by dividing total cost (the sum of fixed cost and variable cost) by the quantity of output produced; equivalently, it equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. For example, with a fixed cost of $1,000 and a variable cost of $500 for 100 units, total cost is $1,500, so average total cost is $15 per unit. If the market price is below average total cost, the firm is losing money on every unit sold on average, since each unit's cost per unit exceeds the revenue per unit it earns. This does not necessarily mean the firm should shut down immediately, though: in the short run, the relevant comparison for the shutdown decision is price versus average variable cost, not average total cost, because fixed costs must be paid whether the firm produces or not.
