A firm with price below average total cost but above average variable cost should keep operating in the short run, since it is at least covering its variable costs and recovering part of its unavoidable fixed costs, even though it is suffering an economic loss overall; in the long run, however, persistent price below average total cost signals that firms should exit the industry. Glossary. Chapter 5: Production and Costs

docs.title: How do you use the shutdown rule to decide whether a competitive firm should keep producing in the short run?
docs.text: The shutdown rule states that a firm should stop producing in the short run if the price it receives is less than its average variable cost, since it would lose less money by shutting down (losing only its unavoidable fixed costs) than by operating (losing fixed costs plus the gap between price and variable cost on every unit). To apply it, compare the current market price to the firm's average variable cost at the output level where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. If price is above average variable cost, even if it is below average total cost, the firm should keep producing, because it is covering all of its variable costs and recovering at least part of its fixed costs, which is better than covering none of them by shutting down. If price falls below average variable cost, the firm should shut down temporarily, since continuing to operate would mean losing money on every single unit produced, beyond just the unavoidable fixed costs. For example, a firm facing a price below its average variable cost shuts down rather than operate, because continuing to produce would lose even more than its unavoidable fixed costs alone. This rule only applies in the short run; in the long run, a firm comparing price to average total cost should exit the industry entirely if it cannot cover all its costs. Glossary. Chapter 6: Perfect Competition

docs.title: How do you tell whether demand is elastic, inelastic, or unit-elastic from the price elasticity number?
docs.text: Take the absolute value of the calculated price elasticity of demand and compare it to 1. If the absolute value is greater than 1, demand is elastic, meaning quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than the price change that caused it. If the absolute value is less than 1, demand is inelastic, meaning quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than the price change. If the absolute value is exactly 1, demand is unit-elastic, meaning the percentage change in quantity demanded exactly equals the percentage change in price. Two further special cases sit at the extremes: perfectly elastic demand, represented by a horizontal demand curve, where buyers will purchase any amount at one specific price but none at all at any higher price; and perfectly inelastic demand, represented by a vertical demand curve, where quantity demanded does not change at all regardless of the price charged. A useful shortcut that avoids calculating elasticity directly is the total revenue test: if raising price causes total revenue to fall, demand is elastic over that range; if raising price causes total revenue to rise, demand is inelastic over that range; and if total revenue stays the same, demand is unit-elastic. Glossary. Chapter 3: Elasticity

docs.title: How do you calculate producer surplus and consumer surplus from a market diagram?
docs.text: On a standard supply-and-demand diagram with the equilibrium price and quantity marked, consumer surplus is the area of the triangle bounded above by the demand curve, below by the horizontal line at the equilibrium price, and on the right by the vertical line at the equilibrium quantity; it represents the total extra value buyers received beyond what they actually paid, summed across every unit sold. Producer surplus is the mirror-image triangle: bounded below by the supply curve, above by the horizontal line at the equilibrium price, and on the right by the vertical line at the equilibrium quantity; it represents the total extra revenue sellers received beyond the minimum they would have accepted, summed across every unit sold. For simple linear demand and supply curves, each triangle's area can be calculated using the standard triangle-area formula, one-half times base times height, where the base is the equilibrium quantity and the height is the vertical distance between the equilibrium price and where the relevant curve meets the vertical price axis (for consumer surplus) or the quantity axis origin price (for producer surplus). Adding the two triangles together gives total surplus, the standard measure of the overall gains from trade a market generates at equilibrium. Glossary. Chapter 2: Supply and Demand

docs.title: How do economies of scale and diseconomies of scale together shape the long-run average cost curve's U-shape?
docs.text: At low levels of output, a firm typically experiences economies of scale: long-run average cost falls as output rises, because fixed investments like specialized machinery get spread over more units, and larger scale often allows bulk input discounts and worker specialization. This creates the initial downward-sloping portion of the U-shaped long-run average cost curve. As output keeps growing, the firm eventually reaches its minimum efficient scale, the output level where long-run average cost reaches its lowest point. Beyond that point, many firms experience diseconomies of scale: long-run average cost starts rising again as output grows further, typically due to coordination and management difficulties that come with running a very large organization, such as added layers of management slowing decision-making and raising costs per unit. The combination of falling average cost at low output (economies of scale) and rising average cost at very high output (diseconomies of scale) is exactly what produces the characteristic U-shape, and the width of the flat bottom of that U, how large a range of output achieves close to the minimum cost, helps explain real-world industry structure: industries with a very wide efficient range, like utilities, tend toward natural monopoly, while industries with a narrow efficient range tend to support many competing firms. Glossary. Chapter 5: Production and Costs

docs.title: What's the difference between first-degree, second-degree, and third-degree price discrimination, and how does the information each requires differ?
docs.text: First-degree price discrimination charges each individual buyer the maximum price that specific buyer is willing to pay, capturing all consumer surplus as profit; a car salesperson who negotiates a separate, maximum price with each customer individually is attempting first-degree discrimination, and it requires the seller to know, or successfully negotiate out, each buyer's individual willingness to pay, which is informationally demanding and rarely achieved perfectly in practice. Second-degree price discrimination offers different prices or terms based on the quantity purchased or the version of the product chosen, letting buyers sort themselves into price categories; a phone company offering cheaper per-gigabyte rates on larger data plans is practicing second-degree discrimination, and it requires much less information, since the seller designs a menu of options and buyers self-select based on their own usage patterns, without the seller needing to know each buyer individually. Third-degree price discrimination charges different prices to distinct groups of customers identified by an observable characteristic, such as age or location; airlines charging different fares for business travelers versus leisure travelers who book well in advance are practicing third-degree discrimination, requiring only that the seller can identify group membership, such as a student ID, not individual willingness to pay. Glossary. Chapter 7: Monopoly

docs.title: What is the midpoint elasticity formula, and why do economists use it instead of simple percentage changes?
docs.text: The midpoint elasticity formula calculates price elasticity of demand by dividing the percentage change in quantity by the percentage change in price, but it computes each percentage change by dividing the raw change by the average (midpoint) of the initial and final values, rather than by only the initial value. Economists use this version specifically because a simple percentage change calculated from the initial value gives a different, inconsistent elasticity depending on whether price is rising or falling between the same two points; for example, going from $10 to $8 is a 20% decrease using $10 as the base, but going from $8 back to $10 is a 25% increase using $8 as the base, even though it is the exact same two points on the demand curve. The midpoint formula fixes this inconsistency by using the same average value as the denominator in both directions, so the calculated elasticity between any two points is identical whether you are moving from the first point to the second or from the second back to the first. This matters in practice whenever a problem does not clearly tell you which price is the "starting" price, which is common, since the midpoint formula removes the ambiguity about which direction you are supposedly moving. Glossary. Chapter 3: Elasticity

docs.title: Why do students often confuse "elastic" with "big demand," and what does elasticity actually measure?
docs.text: A very common misconception is thinking that "elastic demand" means a good is in high demand or popular, or that "inelastic" means a good is unpopular. In fact, elasticity has nothing to do with how much of a good is purchased in absolute terms; it measures only how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price, that is, the ratio of a percentage change in quantity to a percentage change in price. A good can have enormous total demand, meaning huge quantities are purchased, while still having highly elastic demand if buyers would sharply cut back purchases in response to even a small price increase. For example, demand for a specific brand of soda can be very high in absolute terms, with millions of cans sold, while still being elastic, since buyers can easily switch to another brand the moment its price rises noticeably. Conversely, demand for insulin is inelastic, meaning quantity barely changes with price, even though total quantity purchased might be modest relative to a mass-market product. The accurate mental model is: elasticity describes the shape and steepness of the responsiveness relationship, not the size or popularity of the market, and the two concepts are measured completely independently of one another. Glossary. Chapter 3: Elasticity

docs.title: What is the tangency condition in consumer theory, and what does it mean geometrically?
docs.text: The tangency condition is the requirement that, at the consumer optimum, the budget line just touches the highest attainable indifference curve without crossing it, so the marginal rate of substitution equals the ratio of the two goods' prices. Geometrically, this means the slope of the indifference curve (the marginal rate of substitution, the rate at which the consumer is willing to trade one good for the other while staying equally satisfied) exactly equals the slope of the budget line (the negative of the ratio of the two goods' prices) at the chosen bundle. If the two slopes are not equal at a particular point on the budget line, the consumer is not yet at the optimum: she could trade along the budget line, giving up some of one good for more of the other, and reach a higher indifference curve while still staying within her budget. Students often find this condition hard because it combines two separate curves (an indifference curve representing preferences and a straight budget line representing what is affordable) and asks for the one point where their slopes match exactly, rather than, say, where they intersect at all (which happens at many points) or where total utility is highest in isolation. Practicing by sketching several indifference curves crossing a single budget line, and visually identifying the one tangent point, builds the geometric intuition faster than algebra alone. Glossary. Chapter 4: Consumer Theory

docs.title: What is a Nash equilibrium, and why isn't it necessarily the best outcome for the players?
docs.text: A Nash equilibrium is a situation in a game in which every player is choosing the best strategy available given the strategies chosen by all other players, so no single player can benefit by changing their own strategy alone, holding everyone else's strategy fixed. The key word is "alone": a Nash equilibrium only requires that no individual player regrets their choice unilaterally, not that the outcome is good for the players collectively, or even that any player is actually happy with the result. This is exactly what makes the prisoner's dilemma so unsettling: both players confessing is a Nash equilibrium, since neither player can improve their own outcome by switching strategies while the other stays put, yet both players would have been strictly better off if they had both stayed silent instead. The reason staying silent together is not a Nash equilibrium is that each player, individually, could improve their own payoff by confessing while the other stays silent, so the "both cooperate" outcome is unstable even though it is mutually preferable. Students sometimes mistakenly treat Nash equilibrium as a synonym for "the best possible outcome," but it is better understood as "the self-consistent outcome once everyone is behaving in their own rational self-interest," which can diverge sharply from the group-optimal outcome. Glossary. Chapter 10: Game Theory

docs.title: Why does a Pigouvian tax fix a negative externality instead of just banning the activity?
docs.text: A Pigouvian tax is a tax levied on an activity that generates a negative externality, set equal to the external cost per unit, in order to align private incentives with the full social cost of the activity. The goal of correcting a negative externality is not to eliminate the activity entirely, but to reduce it to the socially efficient quantity, the level where the social marginal benefit of the activity equals its social marginal cost, including the external cost. A complete ban would eliminate not just the inefficient, overproduced units but also every unit of the activity that is still genuinely worth doing even after accounting for its external cost, destroying real value in the process. A Pigouvian tax, by contrast, raises the private cost of the activity by exactly the size of the external cost, so each producer or consumer now faces the true social cost of their decision and will naturally cut back only on the units whose benefit no longer exceeds the full social cost, while continuing units that are still worthwhile overall. For example, a tax on each ton of carbon emitted is a Pigouvian tax designed to make polluters pay for the climate damage their emissions cause to others, discouraging excessive pollution while still allowing economically valuable production to continue at a more efficient, lower level. Glossary. Chapter 13: Externalities and Public Goods

docs.title: How do you calculate price elasticity of demand using the midpoint formula, step by step?
docs.text: First, identify the initial price and quantity (P1, Q1) and the new price and quantity (P2, Q2) from the problem. Second, calculate the percentage change in quantity using the midpoint formula: divide the change in quantity (Q2 − Q1) by the average of the two quantities ((Q1 + Q2) divided by 2), then multiply by 100. Third, calculate the percentage change in price the same way: divide the change in price (P2 − P1) by the average of the two prices ((P1 + P2) divided by 2), then multiply by 100. Fourth, divide the percentage change in quantity by the percentage change in price to get the elasticity value. For example, if price rises from $8 to $12 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 60 units, the percentage change in quantity is (60 − 100) divided by 80, equal to −50%, and the percentage change in price is (12 − 8) divided by 10, equal to 40%. Dividing −50% by 40% gives an elasticity of −1.25, which in absolute value is greater than 1, so demand is elastic over this price range. A common mistake is forgetting to use the average (midpoint) values in the denominators and instead using only the initial values, which produces an inconsistent elasticity depending on the direction of the price change. Glossary. Chapter 3: Elasticity

docs.title: How do you find the consumer optimum using the tangency condition between the budget line and an indifference curve?
docs.text: Start by drawing the consumer's budget line, a straight line whose slope is the negative of the ratio of the two goods' prices and whose endpoints are determined by the consumer's income divided by each good's price. Then sketch a family of indifference curves, each representing a constant level of satisfaction, with curves farther from the origin representing higher satisfaction. The consumer optimum is the single point where one of these indifference curves is tangent to the budget line, touching it at exactly one point without crossing it, since this is the highest indifference curve the consumer can reach while staying within budget. Algebraically, you find this point by setting the marginal rate of substitution (the slope of the indifference curve) equal to the price ratio (the slope of the budget line), and solving that equation together with the budget constraint equation simultaneously, since you have two unknowns, the quantity of each good, and need two equations to solve for them. For example, if a consumer's marginal rate of substitution equals the ratio of apple price to orange price at a particular bundle, and that bundle also satisfies the budget constraint exactly, that bundle is the consumer optimum. Any point where the two slopes are not yet equal is not optimal, since the consumer could still trade along the budget line to reach a higher indifference curve. Glossary. Chapter 4: Consumer Theory

docs.title: How do you find the Nash equilibrium in a payoff matrix?
docs.text: Use the "best response" method. First, for each strategy the column player might choose, identify the row player's best response, the strategy that gives the row player the highest payoff given that specific column choice, and mark it. Second, for each strategy the row player might choose, identify the column player's best response the same way, and mark it. Third, look for any cell in the matrix where both players' strategies are marked as a best response to each other simultaneously; that cell is a Nash equilibrium, since neither player would want to deviate unilaterally. A payoff matrix can have exactly one Nash equilibrium, multiple Nash equilibria (common in coordination games), or, in simultaneous games without repetition, sometimes no equilibrium in pure strategies at all. For example, in a classic prisoner's dilemma payoff matrix, checking all four cells reveals that "both confess" is the only cell where each player's strategy is a best response to the other's, making it the unique Nash equilibrium, even though "both stay silent" would give both players a better outcome. A useful shortcut: if a player has a dominant strategy, a strategy that is their best response no matter what the other player does, you can immediately mark every cell in that player's row or column consistent with playing it, which quickly narrows down where the equilibrium must be. Glossary. Chapter 10: Game Theory

docs.title: How do you solve a sequential game using backward induction?
docs.text: Backward induction solves a sequential game by analyzing the very last decision in the game first, determining what the player making that final move would rationally do given everything that has already happened, and then working backward one step at a time through earlier decisions, each time assuming later players will behave exactly as already determined. Concretely, draw the game as a decision tree with branches representing each player's possible choices at each stage, and payoffs listed at the end of every branch. Start at the final decision nodes, nearest the payoffs, and circle whichever choice gives the player at that node the higher payoff, eliminating the other branch. Move up one level to the previous decision node, and now, knowing exactly what will happen at every later node because you just solved it, determine the best choice at this earlier node given those known later outcomes. Repeat until you reach the very first decision at the top of the tree. For example, using backward induction, an entrant predicts how an incumbent firm would actually respond to entry (by solving the incumbent's decision first), and then makes its own entry decision based on that predicted response, rather than being swayed by a threat the incumbent would not actually find profitable to carry out, which the course calls a non-credible threat. Glossary. Chapter 10: Game Theory

docs.title: How do you calculate the size of a deadweight loss triangle on a supply-and-demand diagram?
docs.text: Deadweight loss appears on a diagram as a triangle sitting between the demand curve and the supply curve, bounded on one side by the efficient (competitive equilibrium) quantity and on the other side by the actual, distorted quantity that results from a tax, price control, or monopoly restriction. To calculate its area, use the standard triangle-area formula: one-half times the base times the height. The base of the triangle is the horizontal distance between the efficient quantity and the actual quantity, that is, how many units of trade were lost. The height of the triangle is the vertical gap at the actual quantity between the demand curve (what buyers would be willing to pay for that marginal unit) and the supply curve (what it would cost to supply that marginal unit), which represents the per-unit surplus that each lost unit would have generated had it been traded. For example, if a tax reduces quantity traded from 100 units to 80 units, and at 80 units buyers would pay $12 while sellers would need $8 to supply it, the deadweight loss triangle has a base of 20 units and a height of $4, giving an area of one-half times 20 times 4, equal to $40 of lost total surplus. Glossary. Chapter 7: Monopoly

docs.title: Why does the prisoner's dilemma produce a worse outcome for both players even though each is behaving rationally?
docs.text: The prisoner's dilemma is a game in which each player has a dominant strategy that leads to a worse outcome for both players collectively than if they had cooperated instead, illustrating a direct conflict between individual rationality and group interest. Each player, reasoning entirely rationally and selfishly, compares their own payoff from each possible strategy against every possible choice the other player might make, and finds that one strategy, call it defecting or confessing, always gives them a strictly higher personal payoff no matter what the other player does. Because this logic applies symmetrically to both players, both rationally choose to defect, landing on the Nash equilibrium. The tragedy is that if both players had instead chosen to cooperate, both would have received a higher payoff than they get at the Nash equilibrium, but neither player can unilaterally choose that better outcome, because whichever one tries to cooperate while the other defects ends up with the worst individual payoff of all. For example, two firms that would both profit more by keeping prices high end up competing them down because each individually gains by undercutting the other, even though both would prefer the high-price outcome if they could somehow trust each other to stick with it. This tension is exactly why real-world oligopolies attempt collusion, and why repeated interaction and strategies like tit-for-tat can sometimes sustain cooperation that a single, one-shot game cannot. Glossary. Chapter 10: Game Theory

docs.title: How does information asymmetry explain why insurance markets can suffer from both adverse selection and moral hazard at the same time?
docs.text: Information asymmetry means one party to a transaction has more or better information than the other, and insurance markets involve two distinct information gaps that create two distinct problems simultaneously. Before a policy is purchased, applicants know their own health, driving habits, or risk level far better than the insurer does, which creates adverse selection: at any given premium, people who already know they are higher risk are more likely to find that premium worthwhile and buy coverage, while lower-risk people are more likely to decline, skewing the pool of buyers toward higher average risk than the insurer priced for. After a policy is purchased, the insurer can no longer closely observe the policyholder's ongoing behavior, which creates moral hazard: knowing that the insurer will cover most losses, the insured person has a weaker incentive to take costly precautions, such as driving carefully or managing their health, than they would without coverage. These two problems compound each other in a way that is genuinely difficult to grasp at first, because they operate at different stages of the same relationship and call for different remedies: adverse selection is addressed by better screening and underwriting before a policy is issued, while moral hazard is addressed by deductibles, co-payments, and monitoring that restore some incentive for caution after coverage begins. Glossary. Chapter 14: Information Economics

docs.title: How should I decide which economic tool, marginal analysis, elasticity, or game theory, fits a given real-world decision?
docs.text: Start by asking whether the decision involves only your own trade-off between an action's benefit and cost, with no other strategic actor reacting to your choice; if so, marginal analysis, comparing marginal benefit to marginal cost, is usually the right starting tool, whether you are a consumer deciding how much to buy or a firm deciding how much to produce. If the decision instead centers on how buyers or sellers will respond to a price change, specifically how much quantity will shift in percentage terms, elasticity is the right tool, since it directly measures that responsiveness and tells you things marginal analysis alone cannot, such as whether raising price will raise or lower total revenue. If the decision instead depends critically on what a rival, competitor, or counterpart will do in response to your own choice, and their best choice similarly depends on yours, you are in a strategic setting and need game theory, dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium, or backward induction for sequential moves, rather than marginal analysis or elasticity alone. In practice, many real decisions require combining tools: a firm might use elasticity to estimate how a price change affects its own demand, and then use game theory to predict whether a rival will match that price change, before applying marginal analysis to find the resulting profit-maximizing choice. Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics

docs.title: How can a business use marginal analysis to decide whether to hire one more worker?
docs.text: A business should hire an additional worker only if that worker's marginal revenue product, the additional revenue generated by their added output, is at least as large as the wage the firm must pay them; this is exactly the labor hiring rule covered in the factor markets chapter. To apply it in practice, estimate how much extra output the next worker would add (their marginal product) and multiply that by the extra revenue each additional unit of output brings in (marginal revenue), giving the marginal revenue product. Compare that figure to the wage rate the firm must pay to attract and retain that worker. If marginal revenue product exceeds the wage, hiring adds to profit and the firm should hire; if it falls below the wage, hiring that worker would reduce profit, and the firm should stop hiring at the current staffing level. For example, a firm should stop hiring once the next worker's marginal revenue product would be only $12 but the prevailing wage rate is $15, since that hire would actually reduce profit rather than increase it, even though the worker would still add some positive output. This same marginal comparison, extended across every additional worker, traces out the firm's entire labor demand curve. Glossary. Chapter 11: Factor Markets

docs.title: How can a manager use price elasticity of demand to decide whether to raise or lower prices?
docs.text: The manager should first estimate (or look up, if available) the price elasticity of demand for their specific product over the relevant price range. If demand is inelastic, meaning the elasticity's absolute value is less than 1, raising price will increase total revenue, since the percentage increase in price outweighs the smaller percentage decrease in quantity sold; conversely, lowering price would decrease total revenue in this case. If demand is elastic, meaning the elasticity's absolute value is greater than 1, raising price will decrease total revenue, since the percentage decrease in quantity demanded outweighs the price increase; lowering price would instead increase total revenue, since the large percentage gain in quantity sold more than compensates for the lower price per unit. A manager can apply the total revenue test directly without even calculating a precise elasticity number, simply by testing a small price change and observing whether total revenue rises or falls. For example, a seller of a product with few close substitutes, like a life-saving medication with inelastic demand, could profitably raise price, while a seller of a product like a specific soda brand, which faces elastic demand because buyers can easily switch brands, would generally see revenue fall if it raised price unilaterally. Pricing decisions should always also weigh costs, competitor reactions, and customer goodwill, not elasticity alone. Glossary. Chapter 3: Elasticity

docs.title: How would you use the MR = MC rule to decide whether a firm should expand or shut down production?
docs.text: To decide whether to expand, compare the marginal revenue and marginal cost of the next unit the firm is considering producing: if marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost, expanding output by that unit adds to profit, and the firm should produce it; the firm should keep expanding output unit by unit until marginal revenue equals marginal cost, which is its profit-maximizing output level, and stop there, since producing further units beyond that point would cost more than they bring in. To decide whether to shut down entirely in the short run, the relevant comparison shifts to price versus average variable cost at that profit-maximizing output: if price exceeds average variable cost, even if it is below average total cost, the firm should keep operating, since it is covering its variable costs and recovering part of its fixed costs; only if price falls below average variable cost should the firm shut down temporarily, since continuing to operate would mean losing money on every unit beyond its unavoidable fixed costs. In the long run, the comparison instead should be price versus average total cost, since every cost becomes avoidable by exiting the industry if the firm cannot break even over the long haul. Working through these two separate comparisons, output level first, then operate-or-shutdown second, keeps the decision from becoming an all-or-nothing judgment call made on gut instinct. Glossary. Chapter 6: Perfect Competition

docs.title: How can game theory help you decide whether to trust a competitor's pricing signal?
docs.text: Game theory encourages you to ask not whether a competitor's announced price or threat sounds credible, but whether it would actually be in that competitor's own rational self-interest to follow through on it once the moment to act actually arrives, which is exactly the logic behind identifying a non-credible threat. Model the situation as a sequential game: lay out your competitor's possible responses to your own pricing decision, and use backward induction to solve for what they would truly find optimal at that later stage, given the payoffs they would actually receive, rather than simply taking their stated intention at face value. For example, an incumbent firm might publicly threaten to start a costly price war against any new entrant, but if backward induction reveals that the price war would actually hurt the incumbent more than simply tolerating modest new competition, that threat is non-credible, and a rational entrant should discount it and enter anyway. Repeated interactions change this calculation: in a repeated game, a firm's credibility can be rebuilt over many rounds through consistent strategies like tit-for-tat, where sticking to a stated pricing policy round after round makes future threats and promises considerably more believable than in a single one-shot interaction. The practical takeaway is to always verify a rival's signal against their own incentives, not their words alone. Glossary. Chapter 10: Game Theory

docs.title: How can a nudge be used to encourage a specific behavior without banning any option?
docs.text: A nudge is a feature of how choices are presented, such as a default option, designed to steer people's decisions in a particular direction without restricting any of the options actually available to them; the policy philosophy behind using nudges deliberately is called libertarian paternalism, favoring choices that are better for people while fully preserving their freedom to choose differently. To design an effective nudge, identify the behavior you want to encourage, then change the default or the presentation of choices so that the desired behavior requires no extra effort, while still leaving every original option fully available to anyone who actively wants it. For example, automatically enrolling new employees in a retirement savings plan, while still letting them opt out at any time, is a nudge: it leverages the common tendency toward inertia (and present bias toward current spending over future saving) to boost retirement saving rates substantially, without legally requiring anyone to participate. Similarly, placing healthier food options at eye level in a cafeteria, while still offering less healthy options elsewhere on the menu, nudges people toward better choices without removing the less healthy options entirely. The key design principle distinguishing a nudge from a mandate or ban is that the person retains complete freedom to opt out or choose otherwise; only the default and the ease of each path have changed. Glossary. Chapter 15: Behavioral Economics

docs.title: How do you analyze whether a market is better served by more competition or by allowing economies of scale to consolidate it?
docs.text: The analysis hinges on comparing the shape of the industry's long-run average cost curve to the size of the market. If a single firm's long-run average cost keeps falling over the entire relevant range of market demand, the industry exhibits natural monopoly conditions, meaning a single large firm can genuinely supply the market more cheaply per unit than several smaller competing firms could; in this case, forcing competition by breaking the firm into many smaller producers would raise average costs for everyone, even though it might appear to increase competition. A single electric grid serving a city is often cited as a natural monopoly for exactly this reason, since building duplicate sets of power lines would be far more costly than one network. If, instead, the minimum efficient scale is small relative to total market demand, meaning many firms can each individually reach their lowest average cost while the market still supports numerous competitors, then promoting competition through antitrust enforcement is more likely to benefit consumers, since competitive pressure will tend to push price down toward marginal cost without sacrificing cost efficiency. The practical move is therefore to estimate where minimum efficient scale falls relative to market size, since that ratio, not an ideological preference for or against competition, should drive the policy recommendation. Chapter 7: Monopoly

docs.title: How should you weigh the trade-offs between a tariff and free trade when evaluating a trade policy?
docs.text: A tariff, a tax imposed on imported goods, raises their price to domestic consumers, protects import-competing domestic producers and the workers they employ, and raises government revenue, but it also creates a tariff welfare loss, a reduction in the country's total surplus caused by distorting trade away from the efficient quantity of imports, beyond whatever revenue the tariff raises. Free trade maximizes a country's total gains from specializing according to comparative advantage, since it lets consumers buy at the lowest world price and lets domestic producers specialize in whatever they can produce most efficiently relative to other countries, but it also exposes certain groups, particularly workers in import-competing industries, to real and sometimes painful adjustment costs, a phenomenon the course calls trade winners and losers. Weighing this trade-off well requires being explicit about both efficiency and equity criteria rather than only one: on pure efficiency grounds, free trade nearly always generates larger total gains than a tariff, but a policymaker also has to weigh whether the losses borne by specific groups, such as displaced factory workers, are severe enough and concentrated enough to justify either temporary protection (as in the infant industry argument) or direct compensation through programs like trade adjustment assistance, rather than a blanket tariff that sacrifices overall efficiency to protect a narrower group. Glossary. Chapter 16: International Trade

docs.title: How do you analyze whether a given market failure is better addressed by a Pigouvian tax, a subsidy, or a quantity-based tool like cap-and-trade?
docs.text: Start by identifying which direction the externality runs: a negative externality, where the market overproduces relative to the efficient quantity, calls for a Pigouvian tax, set equal to the marginal external cost, to discourage excess production; a positive externality, where the market underproduces, calls for a Pigouvian subsidy, set equal to the marginal external benefit, to encourage more of the activity. Once you know the direction, the choice between a price-based tool (a Pigouvian tax) and a quantity-based tool (cap-and-trade) typically comes down to which one you can set more confidently and how much uncertainty exists about costs. A Pigouvian tax is easier to use when you are confident about the per-unit external cost but uncertain about how costly it will be for different polluters to reduce their emissions, since a fixed tax lets each firm with a different marginal abatement cost choose its own response. Cap-and-trade is easier to use when you want certainty over the total quantity of pollution allowed, since the cap directly fixes the aggregate outcome, while still letting the market, through trading permits, find the cheapest way to distribute the required reductions among firms with different abatement costs. In practice, this means you should ask whether price certainty or quantity certainty matters more for the specific externality at hand before choosing between the two tools. Glossary. Chapter 13: Externalities and Public Goods

docs.title: How do you evaluate whether a monopoly's higher price is justified by its lower costs, as in the case of a natural monopoly?
docs.text: Evaluating this requires comparing two separate effects that pull in opposite directions: the deadweight loss created by the monopoly restricting output and pricing above marginal cost, versus the genuine cost savings created by economies of scale that make a single large producer cheaper per unit than multiple smaller competing producers would be. For a natural monopoly, where long-run average cost keeps falling over the entire relevant range of market demand, forcing the market open to several competing firms would mean each firm operates at a smaller, less efficient scale, raising the average cost of production for everyone, even though competition would otherwise push price closer to marginal cost. The standard policy evaluation weighs this trade-off using regulation rather than simply accepting the unregulated monopoly outcome or forcing in competition: marginal-cost pricing regulation sets price equal to marginal cost to fully eliminate the deadweight loss, achieving allocative efficiency, but it can cause the firm financial losses if marginal cost lies below average total cost at that quantity, often requiring a government subsidy; average-cost pricing regulation instead sets price equal to average total cost, letting the firm break even without a subsidy, though output remains below the fully efficient level. Choosing between these regulatory approaches, rather than between monopoly and forced competition, is usually the more defensible evaluation for a genuine natural monopoly. Glossary. Chapter 7: Monopoly

docs.title: How would you evaluate the welfare effects of different types of price discrimination from a consumer's perspective?
docs.text: Consumers are generally worse off under first-degree price discrimination, since a seller charging each buyer their own maximum willingness to pay captures the entirety of consumer surplus as profit, leaving buyers with none of the gains from trade they would keep in a single-price market, even though total output, and therefore total surplus, may actually be higher than under simple monopoly pricing because the seller no longer restricts output to protect a single high price. Second-degree price discrimination tends to have mixed effects: it can benefit high-usage or budget-conscious consumers who take advantage of bulk discounts or lower-cost product versions, while buyers who do not fit neatly into the offered menu may pay more than they would under a single uniform price. Third-degree price discrimination, charging different prices to identifiable groups, can genuinely benefit the group that receives the lower price, such as students paying less for movie tickets, while making the group charged the higher price worse off than under a single uniform price; whether total consumer welfare rises or falls overall depends on the specific elasticities of the different groups and the respective sizes of the group discounts versus group surcharges. A full evaluation should therefore distinguish which specific group of consumers is being asked about, rather than treating "consumers" as a single, uniformly affected group. Glossary. Chapter 7: Monopoly

docs.title: How would you design a policy proposal that addresses a specific negative externality using the tools from this course?
docs.text: A strong policy proposal starts by clearly identifying the externality: who is the third party bearing the uncompensated cost, what is the activity generating it, and roughly how large is the marginal external cost per unit of that activity. Next, estimate the socially efficient quantity of the activity, the level where social marginal cost, the firm's private marginal cost plus the marginal external cost, equals social marginal benefit, and compare it to the current, inefficient market quantity to size the externality deadweight loss being created. From there, choose a policy tool and justify it explicitly: a Pigouvian tax set equal to the marginal external cost if you want price certainty and are comfortable letting the market determine the resulting quantity; a cap-and-trade system if you want quantity certainty and are willing to let the market determine the resulting price through permit trading; or, if transaction costs between the parties are low and property rights can be clearly assigned, consider whether a Coase theorem solution, letting the affected parties negotiate directly, might resolve the externality without government intervention at all. Finally, address likely objections using efficiency and equity criteria together: explain who bears the cost of your proposed policy, whether it might risk government failure (such as a weak tax being captured or watered down by lobbying), and why your chosen tool outperforms the alternatives for this specific externality. Glossary. Chapter 13: Externalities and Public Goods

docs.title: How would you apply game theory concepts to analyze pricing behavior in an oligopoly?
docs.text: Begin by identifying which specific oligopoly model best fits the competitive variable firms actually choose: if firms compete primarily by choosing output quantities, the Cournot model applies, where each firm picks a quantity based on a best-response function that accounts for how much its rival is expected to produce, and the resulting Cournot-Nash equilibrium typically yields a price between the competitive and monopoly levels. If firms compete primarily by choosing prices for an identical product, the Bertrand model applies instead, and strikingly, competitive price-cutting between even just two firms can drive price all the way down to marginal cost, the same outcome as perfect competition, a result known as the Bertrand paradox. If firms interact repeatedly over time rather than just once, you should also model the pricing game as a repeated game, since strategies like tit-for-tat can sustain tacit collusion, keeping prices above the competitive level for extended periods, something a single one-shot game cannot achieve. Finally, if firms believe rivals will match price cuts but not price increases, the kinked demand curve model helps explain price stability (firms are reluctant to change price in either direction) even when costs shift modestly, which is a useful complement to the Cournot and Bertrand frameworks for explaining real-world oligopoly pricing patterns observed across industries like airlines or wireless carriers. Glossary. Chapter 9: Oligopoly

docs.title: How does information economics help explain why insurance markets and used-car markets suffer from similar problems despite being completely different industries?
docs.text: Both markets share the same underlying structural problem, information asymmetry, even though the products being traded could not be more different. In the market for lemons, the classic used-car model, sellers of used cars know the true quality of their own car far better than buyers do, so buyers, unable to tell good cars from bad ones, offer only an average price, which discourages owners of genuinely good used cars from selling at all, leaving mostly low-quality "lemons" in the market. In health or auto insurance, buyers know their own risk level far better than the insurer does, so an insurer offering a single average premium attracts disproportionately higher-risk applicants, the same adverse selection dynamic, potentially spiraling toward an adverse selection death spiral as healthier participants exit and prices keep climbing. The common thread across both markets is that the less-informed party cannot distinguish quality (or risk) and therefore cannot price it correctly, which drives good-quality participants out of the market in both cases. Both markets also share remedies drawn from the same toolkit: signaling, where the informed party takes a costly action to credibly prove their quality (a seller providing a vehicle history report, or a healthy applicant submitting to a medical exam), and screening, where the less-informed party designs a menu of options that different types self-select into, revealing their private information indirectly. Glossary. Chapter 14: Information Economics

docs.title: How do the gains from international trade based on comparative advantage connect to the way factor markets determine wages domestically?
docs.text: International trade theory, especially the Heckscher-Ohlin model, predicts that countries export goods relying heavily on the production factors they have in relative abundance and import goods relying on factors they have relatively less of, which directly affects domestic factor markets because trade changes the derived demand for labor and capital in each industry. When a country opens to trade and specializes according to comparative advantage, demand for labor rises in its expanding, comparative-advantage industries and falls in its contracting, import-competing industries, shifting each industry's labor demand curve and therefore the wage and employment level determined in that specific labor market, exactly the same marginal-revenue-product logic from the factor markets chapter, just driven by a change originating in trade policy rather than domestic technology. This is also the microeconomic root of trade winners and losers: workers whose skills are specific to an expanding export industry see rising labor demand and wages, while workers in a contracting import-competing industry see falling labor demand and wages, even though the country's total gains from trade are positive overall. Factor-price equalization theory takes this connection even further, predicting that as countries trade more freely, wages for similarly skilled workers across trading countries should tend to converge over time, since trade in goods functions as an indirect substitute for the cross-border movement of the underlying factors themselves. Glossary. Chapter 16: International Trade

docs.title: How would you evaluate whether behavioral economics findings like loss aversion and present bias justify "nudge" policies over traditional taxes and subsidies?
docs.text: Evaluating this requires weighing what each policy tool assumes about human decision-making and comparing it to actual evidence about where people systematically deviate from the idealized, perfectly rational consumer assumed in classical models like consumer theory in Chapter 4. Traditional taxes and subsidies, such as a Pigouvian tax, work by changing the relative price of an option, which classical theory assumes is sufficient because rational consumers always respond correctly to price signals; but behavioral economics findings such as loss aversion, present bias, and bounded rationality show that people often respond inconsistently to logically equivalent price changes depending on how those changes are framed, and that people frequently act against their own long-run interests due to time-inconsistent preferences, like repeatedly postponing retirement saving despite planning not to. A nudge, by contrast, works directly on the cognitive bias or default behavior causing the mismatch, for instance addressing procrastination directly through automatic enrollment, rather than only indirectly through price. The honest evaluation is that nudges and price-based tools are not mutually exclusive but address different failure modes: nudges are particularly well suited to problems rooted in defaults, framing, and self-control, where changing a price might not even register strongly in someone's decision, while taxes and subsidies remain more directly suited to externality problems where the core issue is a missing or mispriced cost, not a cognitive bias. The strongest policies often combine both. Glossary. Chapter 15: Behavioral Economics

docs.title: How would you evaluate the claim that free trade always makes a country better off, given that it can still create domestic winners and losers?
docs.text: The claim is true in an important, specific sense and overstated in another: free trade reliably increases a country's total gains from trade, the aggregate size of the economic pie, because specializing according to comparative advantage lets the country, and its trading partners, collectively consume more than if each tried to produce everything domestically, a result the Ricardian trade model demonstrates rigorously. But "the country" is not a single decision-maker; it is made up of distinct groups, some of whom work in expanding export industries and clearly gain, and others who work in contracting import-competing industries and can be made genuinely worse off, even as the economy as a whole gains, exactly the trade winners and losers pattern the course highlights. Evaluating the claim fairly therefore requires separating the efficiency question (does total surplus rise? yes, in standard trade models) from the distributional question (does every individual gain? no, not without some further redistribution). This is why serious evaluations of trade policy pair free trade with explicit attention to the losers, for example through trade adjustment assistance programs that use part of the aggregate gains to compensate or retrain displaced workers, rather than assuming the aggregate gain alone settles the political or ethical question of whether a specific trade agreement is good policy for everyone affected by it. Glossary. Chapter 16: International Trade

docs.title: How would you design a complete policy response to climate change that draws on both externality theory and behavioral economics?
docs.text: A complete design starts with the externality framework: carbon emissions impose a marginal external cost on the rest of society in the form of climate damage, so the core policy tool should be either a Pigouvian tax, a tax on each ton of carbon emitted set equal to the external cost, or a cap-and-trade system, which fixes the total quantity of allowed emissions and lets a market in tradable permits find the cheapest way to achieve that reduction across firms with different marginal abatement costs. On top of this efficiency-based foundation, a well-designed policy should also incorporate behavioral economics insights, since individual decisions about energy use, home insulation, or transportation choices are often driven by present bias (discounting future energy savings too heavily relative to today's upfront cost) and defaults (sticking with whatever energy plan or appliance setting came pre-installed) rather than a careful marginal-benefit-versus-marginal-cost calculation alone. Pairing the Pigouvian tax or cap-and-trade system with well-designed nudges, such as making energy-efficient options the default choice when purchasing appliances or enrolling in utility programs, while preserving consumer choice under libertarian paternalism, can push behavior further toward the efficient outcome than a price signal alone, especially for decisions where present bias causes consumers to systematically undervalue future costs and benefits relative to their true present value. Such a policy should also include transitional support, akin to trade adjustment assistance, for workers and regions economically dependent on high-carbon industries. Glossary. Chapter 13: Externalities and Public Goods

docs.title: How would you build an argument connecting market structure, game theory, and antitrust policy to explain why some industries attract more government scrutiny than others?
docs.text: The argument starts with market structure: industries with few large firms, oligopolies, create strategic interdependence, meaning each firm's pricing and output decisions depend directly on its rivals' decisions, unlike perfectly competitive or even monopolistically competitive industries made up of many small, independent decision-makers. Game theory then explains why this structural feature specifically worries antitrust regulators: a small number of interacting firms can potentially reach a Nash equilibrium involving tacit or explicit collusion, especially in a repeated game where strategies like tit-for-tat allow firms to sustain cooperative, above-competitive pricing over many rounds without ever needing a formal, provably illegal agreement. Measures like the concentration ratio and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index give regulators quantifiable tools to flag exactly which industries have concentrated enough market structure for this strategic dynamic to be a realistic concern, which is why antitrust policy, including oligopoly-specific antitrust policy and historical tools like the Sherman Antitrust Act, focuses disproportionate scrutiny on concentrated industries and proposed mergers that would increase concentration further, while leaving fragmented, monopolistically competitive industries like restaurants or hair salons largely unscrutinized. The connecting thread across all three layers is that structure (few firms) enables a strategic dynamic (interdependence, modeled by game theory) that threatens the policy goal (competitive pricing), which is exactly why antitrust enforcement targets market structure and firm conduct together rather than either one alone. Glossary. Chapter 9: Oligopoly

docs.title: How would you construct an original numerical example showing how asymmetric information could cause a monopsony-like labor market to also suffer from adverse selection?
docs.text: Consider a single rural hospital that is the only major employer of nurses in its region, making it a monopsony in the local labor market: suppose the competitive wage for nurses with observable average skill would be $35 per hour, but because the hospital is the sole buyer, it follows the monopsony hiring rule, hiring only up to the point where the marginal revenue product of the next nurse equals the marginal cost of labor, resulting in a lower posted wage of, say, $28 per hour and fewer nurses hired than a competitive market would support. Now add an information problem: suppose nursing skill varies, and the hospital cannot fully observe each individual applicant's true skill level before hiring, only applicants' own private information about themselves. At a wage of $28, the most skilled nurses, who could earn more in a competitive market elsewhere or in a different profession entirely, are the ones most likely to decline the position or leave quickly, while lower-skilled nurses, with fewer outside options, are more likely to accept and stay, a selection pattern directly analogous to the market for lemons. The hospital's monopsony wage-setting, meant simply to capture monopsony profit through a lower wage, inadvertently also degrades the average quality of its workforce over time, layering an adverse selection cost on top of the standard monopsony inefficiency of hiring fewer workers than the efficient quantity. Glossary. Chapter 11: Factor Markets

docs.title: Absolute Advantage
docs.text:
The ability to produce more output of a good than another producer using the same amount of resources.

Example: A farmer who can grow 100 bushels of corn per acre has an absolute advantage over a neighbor who grows only 60 bushels per acre on identical land.

docs.title: Accounting Profit
docs.text: The difference between a firm's total revenue and its explicit costs, such as wages, rent, and materials, not including the implicit opportunity cost of owner-supplied resources.

docs.title: Adverse Selection
docs.text:
A problem arising from information asymmetry in which the party with less information ends up disproportionately attracting the riskiest or lowest-quality counterparts before a transaction occurs.

Example: An insurance company offering the same health insurance premium to everyone may attract mostly sicker applicants, since healthier people find the premium less worthwhile, a case of adverse selection.

docs.title: Adverse Selection Death Spiral
docs.text:
A process in which rising prices caused by adverse selection drive out the lowest-risk participants, which raises average risk further and prices even more, potentially unraveling the market entirely.

Example: In a health insurance market, rising premiums driven by sicker enrollees can push healthier people to drop coverage altogether, triggering an adverse selection death spiral that keeps pushing premiums higher.

docs.title: Agency Cost
docs.text:
The cost that arises from the conflict of interest and imperfect monitoring in a principal-agent relationship, including the cost of incentives offered and any residual loss from the agent not acting entirely in the principal's interest.

Example: The expense of auditing a company's managers, plus any profit lost because those managers still pursue some of their own goals, together make up the agency cost.

docs.title: Allocative Efficiency
docs.text:
A condition in which resources are allocated so that producing one more unit of a good provides a benefit to society exactly equal to its cost, meaning price equals marginal cost.

Example: Perfectly competitive markets in long-run equilibrium achieve allocative efficiency because price settles where it equals marginal cost.

docs.title: Antitrust Policy
docs.text:
Government laws and enforcement actions aimed at preventing monopoly power, breaking up excessive market concentration, and prohibiting anti-competitive business practices.

Example: A government blocking a merger between two large competing companies because it would substantially reduce competition is an application of antitrust policy.

docs.title: Arbitrage
docs.text:
The practice of buying a good at a low price in one market and reselling it at a higher price in another, which tends to undermine price discrimination by narrowing price gaps.

Example: If a wholesaler buys a discounted student-priced product and resells it to non-students at a markup, that arbitrage can erode the seller's ability to price discriminate.

docs.title: Average Fixed Cost
docs.text: Fixed cost divided by the quantity of output produced, which falls continuously as output increases.

docs.title: Average Product
docs.text: The total output produced divided by the quantity of a variable input used, measuring output per unit of that input.

docs.title: Average Total Cost
docs.text:
Total cost divided by the quantity of output produced, equal to the sum of average fixed cost and average variable cost.

Example: With a fixed cost of $1,000 and a variable cost of $500 for 100 units, average total cost is $15 per unit.

docs.title: Average Variable Cost
docs.text:
Variable cost divided by the quantity of output produced; it shows the variable cost per unit at a given production level.

Example: If total variable cost is $500 at an output of 100 units, average variable cost is $5 per unit.

docs.title: Average-Cost Pricing Regulation
docs.text: A regulatory approach that requires a monopoly to set its price equal to its average total cost, allowing the firm to break even without earning excess profit, though output remains below the fully efficient level.

docs.title: Backward Induction
docs.text:
A method for solving a sequential game by analyzing the last decisions first and working backward to determine what each player should rationally do at each earlier stage.

Example: Using backward induction, an entrant predicts how the incumbent would respond to entry, and makes its entry decision based on that predicted response.

docs.title: Backward-Bending Labor Supply
docs.text:
A pattern in which a worker's labor supply curve slopes upward at low wages but bends backward at high wages, because the income effect eventually outweighs the substitution effect.

Example: A backward-bending labor supply curve could show a worker increasing hours as wages rise from $15 to $30 per hour, but then reducing hours as the wage rises further to $60.

docs.title: Balance of Payments
docs.text:
A comprehensive record of all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world during a given period, including trade, income flows, and financial investments.

Example: A country's balance of payments tracks not just exports and imports of goods, but also tourist spending, dividends paid to foreign investors, and cross-border purchases of stocks and bonds.

docs.title: Barrier to Entry
docs.text:
An obstacle that prevents or discourages new firms from entering a market and competing with existing firms.

Example: A patent on a new drug is a barrier to entry because it legally prevents other firms from producing the same medicine for a set period.

docs.title: Bertrand Model
docs.text:
A model of oligopoly in which firms simultaneously choose the prices they will charge for an identical product, and consumers buy from the lowest-price seller.

Example: In the Bertrand model, if one firm prices even slightly below another, it captures the entire market, driving fierce price competition.

docs.title: Bertrand Paradox
docs.text:
The result of the Bertrand model that, even with only two firms producing an identical good, competitive price-cutting drives price down to marginal cost, the same outcome as under perfect competition.

Example: The Bertrand paradox shows that having just two competing sellers of an identical product can be enough to eliminate all markup above cost.

docs.title: Bounded Rationality
docs.text:
The idea that people make decisions with limited information, limited time, and limited cognitive ability, rather than through the perfectly rational, unlimited calculation assumed in simple economic models.

Example: A shopper who picks a "good enough" cereal brand after a quick glance at the shelf, rather than calculating the best possible option among hundreds, is exhibiting bounded rationality.

docs.title: Brand Loyalty
docs.text: A buyer's tendency to continue purchasing a particular firm's product even when similar, and sometimes cheaper, alternatives are available.

docs.title: Budget Constraint
docs.text:
The limit on the combinations of goods a consumer can purchase, determined by income and the prices of available goods.

Example: With $20 of income and apples priced at $2 each, a consumer's budget constraint limits her to at most 10 apples if she buys nothing else.

docs.title: Cap-and-Trade
docs.text:
A market-based pollution control system in which the government sets a total limit on emissions and issues tradable permits that firms can buy and sell, letting the market determine the cheapest way to meet the cap.

Example: Under cap-and-trade, a firm that can cut its emissions cheaply might sell its unused permits to a firm facing higher cleanup costs, reducing overall pollution at lower total cost.

docs.title: Cartel
docs.text:
A formal agreement among independent firms in the same industry to coordinate pricing and output in order to act collectively like a monopoly.

Example: An international group of oil-producing countries that meets to set production quotas and influence the world price of oil functions as a cartel.

docs.title: Ceteris Paribus
docs.text: A Latin phrase meaning "other things being equal," used to isolate the effect of one variable by holding all other relevant variables constant.

docs.title: Change in Demand
docs.text: A shift of the entire demand curve to a new position, caused by a change in a determinant of demand other than the good's own price.

docs.title: Change in Supply
docs.text: A shift of the entire supply curve to a new position, caused by a change in a determinant of supply other than the good's own price.

docs.title: Choice
docs.text: A decision to use a limited resource, such as time or money, for one purpose instead of another available purpose.

docs.title: Coase Theorem
docs.text:
The proposition that, when transaction costs are low and property rights are clearly defined, private parties can negotiate their own efficient solution to an externality problem without government intervention.

Example: The Coase theorem suggests that a factory and a nearby laundry harmed by its smoke could reach a private deal, such as the factory paying for better filters, that resolves the externality efficiently on their own.

docs.title: Cognitive Bias
docs.text:
A systematic, predictable pattern of deviation from fully rational judgment or decision-making, often arising from mental shortcuts rather than deliberate error.

Example: Overestimating the chance of a plane crash after seeing news coverage of one is a cognitive bias, since the actual risk has not changed.

docs.title: Collusion
docs.text:
A secret or informal agreement among competing firms to coordinate prices, output, or other decisions in order to increase their joint profits.

Example: Rival gas stations quietly agreeing to all raise prices on the same day, without a formal contract, is an example of collusion.

docs.title: Common-Pool Resource
docs.text:
A good that is rival in consumption but non-excludable, meaning it is difficult to prevent access but one person's use reduces what remains for others.

Example: Fish in an open ocean are a common-pool resource, since anyone can fish there but each fish caught is no longer available to other fishers.

docs.title: Comparative Advantage
docs.text:
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer, regardless of who is more skilled overall.

Example: If a lawyer can also type faster than her assistant but earns far more per hour practicing law, she has a comparative advantage in law, not typing, so she should focus on legal work and leave typing to the assistant.

docs.title: Complement Goods
docs.text:
Two goods for which an increase in the price of one causes a decrease in demand for the other, because the goods are typically used together.

Example: Coffee and coffee creamer are complement goods, so a higher price of coffee tends to decrease demand for creamer.

docs.title: Concentration Ratio
docs.text: A measure of market structure calculated as the combined market share of the largest few firms, usually the top four, in an industry.

docs.title: Congestion Pricing
docs.text:
A policy that charges drivers a fee for using a road or area during periods of heavy traffic, intended to reduce the negative externality of congestion by reflecting its true social cost.

Example: A city charging a toll for driving into its downtown core during rush hour, but not at other times, is using congestion pricing.

docs.title: Consumer Optimum
docs.text:
The combination of goods a consumer chooses that maximizes total satisfaction given the limits of the budget constraint.

Example: A consumer's optimum might be 4 apples and 3 oranges, the affordable bundle that leaves her as satisfied as possible.

docs.title: Consumer Surplus
docs.text:
The difference between the maximum price a buyer is willing to pay for a good and the price actually paid, summed across all buyers.

Example: If a buyer would have paid up to $10 for a shirt but only pays $7, she gains $3 of consumer surplus.

docs.title: Coordination Game
docs.text: A game in which players benefit most by choosing matching strategies, so multiple Nash equilibria exist and the main challenge is agreeing on which one to settle on.

docs.title: Cournot Best-Response Function
docs.text: A rule showing the profit-maximizing quantity for one firm to produce, given a specific quantity choice by its rival, in the Cournot model.

docs.title: Cournot Model
docs.text:
A model of oligopoly in which firms simultaneously choose the quantities they will produce, and the market price adjusts based on total output.

Example: In the Cournot model, two firms each choose how many units to produce, and the combined total determines the price both receive.

docs.title: Cournot-Nash Equilibrium
docs.text:
The pair of quantities in the Cournot model at which each firm is producing its best response to the other firm's quantity, so neither wants to change output unilaterally.

Example: At the Cournot-Nash equilibrium, both firms are satisfied with their output choices given what the other is producing, even though total output is higher than under collusion.

docs.title: Credit Rationing
docs.text: A situation in which lenders limit the amount of credit extended to borrowers, or deny loans altogether, even at the prevailing interest rate, because raising the rate further would attract disproportionately riskier borrowers.

docs.title: Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand
docs.text:
A measure of how much the quantity demanded of one good changes in percentage terms in response to a one-percent change in the price of a different good.

Example: A positive cross-price elasticity between tea and coffee confirms they are substitutes, since a higher coffee price raises demand for tea.

docs.title: Current Account
docs.text: The component of the balance of payments that records a country's trade in goods and services, along with net income earned from foreign investments and net transfer payments, but excluding financial asset transactions.

docs.title: Deadweight Loss
docs.text:
The loss of total surplus to society that occurs when a market produces less than the efficient quantity, often because price exceeds marginal cost.

Example: Monopoly pricing creates a deadweight loss because some mutually beneficial trades between willing buyers and the firm's low production cost never happen.

docs.title: Demand
docs.text:
The willingness and ability of buyers to purchase different quantities of a good at different prices during a given time period.

Example: A consumer's demand for coffee describes how many cups she would buy at $2 each, at $4 each, and so on.

docs.title: Demand Curve
docs.text:
A graph showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity of it that buyers wish to purchase, holding other factors constant, typically sloping downward.

Example: Plotting the price of coffee against cups purchased per week traces out a downward-sloping demand curve.

docs.title: Demand Curve Derivation
docs.text: The process of building an individual demand curve by tracing out the quantity of a good a consumer chooses at each possible price, holding income and other prices constant.

docs.title: Derived Demand
docs.text: The demand for an input, such as labor, that arises from and depends on the demand for the final good or service that input helps produce.

docs.title: Determinants of Demand
docs.text:
The factors other than a good's own price that influence how much of it buyers wish to purchase, including income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, and the number of buyers.

Example: A rise in consumer income is a determinant of demand that can shift the entire demand curve for restaurant meals.

docs.title: Determinants of Price Elasticity
docs.text: The factors that make demand for a good more or less responsive to price changes, including availability of substitutes, the share of income spent on the good, whether it is a necessity or luxury, and the length of the time period considered.

docs.title: Determinants of Supply
docs.text:
Factors other than a good's own price that influence how much of it sellers wish to offer, including input costs, technology, expectations, the number of sellers, and prices of related goods in production.

Example: A new fertilizer that raises crop yields is a determinant of supply that can shift the entire supply curve for wheat.

docs.title: Diminishing Marginal Returns
docs.text:
The tendency for the marginal product of a variable input to eventually decline as more of it is added to a fixed amount of other inputs.

Example: Adding more and more workers to a single kitchen eventually produces smaller and smaller increases in meals served, as workers get in each other's way.

docs.title: Diminishing Marginal Utility
docs.text:
The tendency for the additional satisfaction gained from each successive unit of a good to decline as more of it is consumed.

Example: The first slice of pizza is highly satisfying, but by the fifth slice the added enjoyment is much smaller, illustrating diminishing marginal utility.

docs.title: Diseconomies of Scale
docs.text:
A situation in which long-run average cost rises as a firm increases the scale of its output, often due to coordination and management difficulties in very large organizations.

Example: A company that grows so large that layers of management slow decision-making and raise costs per unit is experiencing diseconomies of scale.

docs.title: Dominant Strategy
docs.text:
A strategy that gives a player the best outcome no matter what strategy the other player chooses.

Example: If a firm earns more profit by advertising whether or not its rival advertises, advertising is the firm's dominant strategy.

docs.title: Dominated Strategy
docs.text: A strategy that gives a player a worse outcome than some other available strategy, regardless of what the other player chooses, and so would never be rationally selected.

docs.title: Economic Model
docs.text: A simplified representation of economic relationships, often using graphs or equations, built to explain or predict behavior by focusing on the most important factors.

docs.title: Economic Profit
docs.text:
The difference between a firm's total revenue and its total costs, including both explicit costs and the implicit opportunity cost of resources the owner supplies, such as forgone wages.

Example: A business owner earning $50,000 in accounting profit but who gave up a $60,000 salaried job to run the business actually has an economic loss of $10,000.

docs.title: Economic Rent
docs.text:
A payment to the owner of a resource, such as land, that is in fixed or nearly fixed supply, in excess of the minimum amount needed to keep that resource in its current use.

Example: Because the total supply of a scenic downtown lot is essentially fixed, much of the high price a business pays to use it is economic rent rather than a cost of producing more of it.

docs.title: Economies of Scale
docs.text:
A situation in which long-run average cost falls as a firm increases the scale of its output.

Example: A car manufacturer that spreads the cost of expensive machinery over a much larger number of vehicles experiences economies of scale.

docs.title: Education Signaling Model
docs.text:
A model in which workers acquire education not necessarily because it increases their productivity, but because it credibly signals existing ability to employers who cannot directly observe that ability.

Example: In the education signaling model, a high-ability worker earns a degree mainly to prove to employers, at relatively low personal cost, an ability that lower-ability workers would find too costly to fake.

docs.title: Elastic Demand
docs.text:
A condition in which quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than the percentage change in price, so price elasticity of demand is greater than one in absolute value.

Example: Demand for a specific brand of soda is often elastic, since buyers can easily switch to another brand if its price rises.

docs.title: Elasticity
docs.text: A general measure of how responsive one economic variable, such as quantity, is to a change in another variable, such as price or income, expressed as a ratio of percentage changes.

docs.title: Endowment Effect
docs.text:
The tendency for people to value something more highly simply because they already own it, compared to the price they would pay to acquire the identical item.

Example: A person who wouldn't pay $20 for a mug but refuses to sell an identical mug they already own for less than $30 is exhibiting the endowment effect.

docs.title: Equal Marginal Principle
docs.text:
The rule that a consumer with a limited budget maximizes total utility by allocating spending so that the marginal utility per dollar spent is equal across all goods purchased.
