docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Explain why the demand for labor and other inputs is a derived demand
  2. Calculate marginal revenue product (MRP) and use it to find a firm's profit-maximizing hiring level
  3. Derive a firm's labor demand curve and explain what shifts it
  4. Analyze the labor supply decision as a work-leisure trade-off
  5. Determine the equilibrium wage and employment level in a competitive labor market
  6. Contrast competitive labor markets with monopsony and explain why monopsony depresses wages and employment
  7. Explain how interest rates allocate capital, and distinguish economic rent from other factor payments

Same Marginal Logic, Brand New Markets

Every choice has a trade-off — and up to now, you've mostly analyzed that trade-off from the seller's side of an output market. This chapter flips the lens: firms become buyers, hiring workers and renting capital, and the same marginal reasoning you already mastered — set marginal benefit equal to marginal cost — explains wages, interest rates, and rents too. You already know more of this chapter than you think.

docs.title: 11.1 Input Markets and Derived Demand
docs.text:
So far we have studied markets for output — the goods and services firms sell to consumers. This chapter turns to markets for the inputs, or factors of production, that firms use to produce that output: labor, capital, land, and entrepreneurship. The prices of these factors — wages, interest rates, rents, and profits — determine how income is distributed across the economy.

Input markets differ from output markets in one crucial way: nobody wants an input for its own sake. A firm does not hire a worker because it enjoys having workers around; it hires a worker because that worker helps produce a good the firm can sell. This gives rise to the concept of derived demand: the demand for an input is derived from the demand for the output it helps produce.

Derived demand in practice

When consumer demand for new housing rises, the demand for construction workers, lumber, and land for development all rise with it — not because anyone values carpenters or two-by-fours intrinsically, but because they are necessary to produce houses. When housing demand collapses (as in 2008), derived demand for construction labor collapses too.

This linkage means every input market is connected to some output market. To understand the labor market for software engineers, you must understand the demand for software; to understand the market for farmland, you must understand the demand for food.

Every Input Curve Has an Output Market Hiding Inside It

Here's the mental model to carry through this whole chapter: nobody ever demands an input for its own sake. Every curve you draw for labor, capital, or land secretly has an output market baked into it — shift the demand for houses, and you've just shifted the demand for construction workers, lumber, and land, whether or not you drew that connection explicitly.

docs.title: Defining MRP
docs.text:
How many workers should a profit-maximizing firm hire? The key concept is marginal revenue product (MRP): the additional revenue a firm earns from employing one more unit of an input.

\[MRP_L = MP_L \times MR\]

where \(MP_L\) is the marginal product of labor (the extra output produced by one more worker) and \(MR\) is the marginal revenue the firm earns from selling one more unit of output. In a perfectly competitive output market, \(MR = P\), so:

\[MRP_L = MP_L \times P\]

MRP tells the firm exactly what an additional worker is worth to it in dollar terms.

docs.title: A Worked Numerical Example
docs.text:
Consider a competitive bakery selling bread at \(P = \$4\) per loaf. The table below shows how output responds as the bakery adds workers, holding its ovens (capital) fixed.

Workers (\(L\)) Total Product (loaves/day) Marginal Product (\(MP_L\)) MRP (\(MP_L \times \$4\)) 0 0 — — 1 20 20 $80 2 36 16 $64 3 48 12 $48 4 56 8 $32 5 60 4 $16 6 60 0 $0

Notice that marginal product falls as more workers are added — this is diminishing marginal returns (Chapter 5), which arises because the fixed number of ovens means each additional worker has less capital to work with.

docs.title: The Hiring Rule
docs.text:
A profit-maximizing firm keeps hiring workers as long as each additional worker adds more to revenue than to cost. The firm hires up to the point where:

\[MRP_L = w\]

where \(w\) is the wage rate. If \(MRP_L > w\), the worker generates more revenue than they cost — hire them. If \(MRP_L < w\), the worker costs more than they generate — do not hire them (or lay them off).

Applying the hiring rule

Suppose the market wage for bakery workers is \(w = \$50\)/day. Using the table above:

  • Hiring the 3rd worker: \(MRP_L = \$48 < \$50\). Not worth it — stop before the 3rd worker.
  • Hiring the 2nd worker: \(MRP_L = \$64 > \$50\). Worth it — hire the 2nd worker.

The bakery hires 2 workers, since that is the largest \(L\) for which \(MRP_L \geq w\). At \(w = \$32\), the bakery would hire 4 workers instead (\(MRP_L = \$32\) at \(L=4\)).

This is the same logic as the MR = MC rule from Chapter 6, applied to an input rather than an output: hire inputs up to the point where the marginal benefit (MRP) equals the marginal cost (the wage).

docs.title: The Labor Demand Curve
docs.text:
Because the hiring rule says "hire until \(MRP_L = w\)," the MRP curve is the firm's labor demand curve. It is downward-sloping because \(MP_L\) diminishes as more labor is added (holding capital fixed).

\[Q_L^d = f(w), \quad \frac{\partial Q_L^d}{\partial w} < 0\]

A market labor demand curve is the horizontal sum of all firms' individual MRP curves in that labor market.

docs.title: What Shifts Labor Demand?
docs.text:
Determinant Effect on Labor Demand Increase in output price (\(P\)) Demand increases (MRP = \(MP_L \times P\) rises) Increase in productivity (\(MP_L\)), e.g., better technology or training Demand increases More capital (complementary input) Demand increases, if capital and labor are complements Automation that substitutes for labor Demand decreases Increase in demand for the final good Demand increases (derived demand)

Technology and labor demand: two directions

A new software tool that lets each accountant process twice as many tax returns raises each accountant's \(MP_L\), shifting labor demand for accountants to the right (more accountants demanded at every wage, assuming the firm cannot shrink too much). But self-checkout kiosks are a direct substitute for cashiers, shifting labor demand for cashiers to the left.

docs.title: The Individual's Decision
docs.text:
Workers must decide how to divide their 24 hours between labor (which earns income to buy goods) and leisure (unpaid time, which they also value). The wage rate \(w\) is the opportunity cost of leisure — every hour not worked is an hour of wages foregone.

A higher wage has two competing effects on how many hours a person chooses to work:

  1. Substitution effect: A higher wage raises the opportunity cost of leisure, inducing people to work more hours (substitute away from leisure toward labor).
  2. Income effect: A higher wage raises income at any given number of hours, making people feel richer and want more leisure (assuming leisure is a normal good), inducing them to work fewer hours.

docs.title: The Backward-Bending Labor Supply Curve
docs.text:
At low wages, the substitution effect typically dominates — as wages rise, people work more. But past some wage level, the income effect can dominate — people are rich enough that they "buy back" leisure time by working less even as wages continue to rise. This produces a labor supply curve that slopes upward at first, then bends backward.

Backward-bending supply in practice

A surgeon earning $500/hour may choose to work fewer hours than one earning $300/hour, if at the higher wage she can meet her desired income target more quickly and prefers additional leisure. Many lottery winners also reduce hours worked, consistent with a pure income effect with no change in the wage at all.

Don't Confuse the Individual Curve With the Market Curve

A common mix-up: assuming every worker's supply curve bends backward, and then confusing that backward-bending individual curve with the upward-sloping market curve covered next. Most workers, most of the time, sit on the ordinary upward-sloping portion — the backward bend is a high-wage phenomenon that shows up for only some workers at some wage levels.

docs.title: Market Labor Supply
docs.text: While an individual's supply curve may bend backward, the market labor supply curve is typically upward-sloping: a higher wage draws new workers into the labor force (increasing labor force participation) even if some existing workers choose to work fewer hours.

docs.title: Finding the Equilibrium Wage
docs.text:
In a competitive labor market — many buyers (firms) and many sellers (workers), none with market power — the equilibrium wage \(w^*\) and employment level \(L^*\) are found just as in Chapter 2, by setting labor demand equal to labor supply:

\[L^d(w) = L^s(w)\]

Solving for equilibrium

Suppose the labor market for baristas in a city has:

\[L^d = 2000 - 100w \qquad L^s = -400 + 150w\]

Setting \(L^d = L^s\):

\[2000 - 100w = -400 + 150w$$ $$2400 = 250w$$ $$w^* = \$9.60/\text{hour}, \qquad L^* = 2000 - 100(9.60) = 1040 \text{ workers}\]

A Ten-Second Check on Any Labor-Market Equilibrium

After solving for \(w^*\), plug it back into the demand equation and the supply equation separately. If they don't land on the same \(L^*\), you made an algebra error somewhere upstream — this quick check catches most mistakes before they cost you the whole problem.

docs.title: Why Wages Differ Across Markets
docs.text:
Competitive labor markets predict a single wage for a homogeneous type of labor. In reality, wages differ enormously across occupations because:

  • Differences in MRP: workers with higher skill or productivity command higher MRP and thus higher wages.
  • Human capital (Section 11.9): education and training raise \(MP_L\).
  • Compensating differentials: unpleasant, dangerous, or inconvenient jobs (night-shift work, offshore oil rigs) must pay more to attract workers, compensating for the non-wage disadvantages.
  • Labor market frictions and discrimination: barriers to entry, imperfect information, and discrimination can prevent wages from equalizing even for similarly productive workers.

docs.title: 11.6 Monopsony: A Single Buyer of Labor
What Is Monopsony?
docs.text:
A monopsony is a market with only one (or a dominant) buyer of an input — the mirror image of a monopoly, which has only one seller of output. Classic examples include a single large factory or hospital that is the overwhelmingly dominant employer in an isolated town, or historically, company towns where one firm owned the mine, the housing, and the store.

Because a monopsonist is the only buyer, it faces the entire upward-sloping market labor supply curve, not a flat wage set by the market. To hire one more worker, it must raise the wage for all its workers, not just the marginal hire. This means the monopsonist's marginal cost of labor (MCL) exceeds the wage:

\[MCL > w\]

Monopsony Is Monopoly's Mirror Image

Notice the symmetry: a monopolist's marginal revenue falls below price because selling one more unit forces the price down on all units sold. A monopsonist's marginal cost of labor rises above the wage because hiring one more worker forces the wage up for all workers already employed. Same underlying mechanic, opposite side of the market.

docs.title: The Monopsony Hiring Rule
docs.text:
A profit-maximizing monopsonist hires where \(MRP_L = MCL\) (marginal benefit equals true marginal cost) — but then pays only the wage on the labor supply curve at that quantity, which is less than \(MRP_L\).

Market Structure Hiring Rule Wage Paid Competitive labor market \(MRP_L = w\) \(w = MRP_L\) Monopsony \(MRP_L = MCL\) \(w < MRP_L\), read off the supply curve

Monopsony depresses both wages and employment

Relative to a competitive labor market, a monopsonist hires fewer workers and pays a lower wage than the competitive outcome. Just as monopoly creates deadweight loss in output markets by restricting output, monopsony creates deadweight loss in input markets by restricting employment.

docs.title: Numerical Example
docs.text:
Suppose a monopsonist faces labor supply \(w = 10 + 0.02L\) (so the wage it must pay rises as it hires more).

Three Small Moves, Not One Big One

If deriving MCL from total labor cost feels like a lot at once, break it into three small moves: multiply wage by \(L\) to get total cost, take one derivative, then set the result equal to \(MRP_L\). It's the same three-move pattern as the Cournot derivation back in Chapter 9 — you've already done this.

Its total labor cost is \(TLC = wL = (10 + 0.02L)L = 10L + 0.02L^2\), so:

\[MCL = \frac{d(TLC)}{dL} = 10 + 0.04L\]

Suppose \(MRP_L = 100 - 0.04L\). Setting \(MRP_L = MCL\):

\[100 - 0.04L = 10 + 0.04L\] \[90 = 0.08L\] \[L^* = 1125\]

The wage paid is read off the supply curve at \(L = 1125\):

\[w^* = 10 + 0.02(1125) = \$32.50\]

But the value of the marginal worker is \(MRP_L = 100 - 0.04(1125) = \$55\). The gap between \(MRP_L = \$55\) and \(w^* = \$32.50\) is the hallmark of monopsony power — the firm pays workers less than the value they create. Had this been a competitive market (hiring where \(MRP_L = w\) directly), employment and wages would both have been higher.

docs.title: Policy Responses
docs.text: A minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage can, in a pure monopsony model (unlike in a competitive market), increase both the wage and employment simultaneously, because it forces the monopsonist closer to the competitive outcome rather than creating a surplus of unhired workers. This is one reason labor economists' views on minimum-wage effects depend heavily on how competitive they believe local labor markets actually are.

docs.title: Capital as a Factor
docs.text: Capital refers to produced inputs used to make other goods — machinery, buildings, and equipment. Firms "rent" capital in the sense of paying for its use, whether they lease it or purchase it with borrowed funds. The interest rate (\(r\)) is the price of capital — more precisely, the price of loanable funds used to finance capital investment.

docs.title: The Investment Decision
docs.text:
A firm invests in a piece of capital if the expected return exceeds the cost of financing it. Formally, a firm should invest in a project as long as:

\[\text{Expected Marginal Rate of Return} \geq r\]

This means capital, like labor, has its own downward-sloping demand curve — the lower the interest rate, the more investment projects become profitable, so the quantity of capital demanded rises as \(r\) falls.

docs.title: Present Value
docs.text:
Because capital investments pay off over time, firms must compare a dollar today with a dollar in the future. The present value (PV) of a future payment \(FV\) received in \(t\) years, discounted at rate \(r\), is:

\[PV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^t}\]

Should the firm buy the machine?

A firm can buy a machine today for $10,000. The machine will generate $11,500 in revenue one year from now, and then be worthless. The market interest rate is 10%.

\[PV = \frac{\$11{,}500}{(1+0.10)^1} = \frac{\$11{,}500}{1.10} = \$10{,}454.55\]

Since the present value of the machine's payoff ($10,454.55) exceeds its $10,000 cost, the firm should buy the machine — the net present value is positive (\(\$454.55\)).

docs.title: Loanable Funds Market
docs.text: The equilibrium interest rate is determined by the supply of loanable funds (household saving) and the demand for loanable funds (firm investment and government borrowing), exactly analogous to the supply-and-demand framework of Chapter 2, with \(r\) playing the role of price.

docs.title: Land Supply Is (Nearly) Fixed
docs.text: Land, in the economic sense, refers to natural resources whose total supply cannot be increased by human effort — most importantly, the physical land itself. Because the aggregate supply of land is essentially fixed regardless of price, the supply curve for land is vertical (perfectly inelastic).

docs.title: Economic Rent
docs.text:
Economic rent is the payment to any factor of production whose supply is fixed (or nearly fixed) — a payment determined entirely by demand, since supply cannot respond. Because supply is vertical, any payment above the bare minimum needed to keep the resource in its current use is pure economic rent; the entire price paid for the use of the land is, in effect, rent.

\[\text{Rent} = \text{entire market-clearing payment, since } Q_s \text{ is fixed}\]

Economic rent for prime farmland

Prime farmland near a growing city has a fixed supply. As the city's population grows, demand for that land rises (both for farming and for development), pushing up the rental price — but no more of this specific land can ever be created. The entire increase in rental price is economic rent: it rewards owning a scarce, fixed resource, not any new cost of production.

The concept of economic rent generalizes beyond literal land: any payment to a resource in excess of what is needed to keep it in its current use — a star athlete's salary beyond what would keep them playing, a uniquely located retail storefront — is also called economic rent.

docs.title: Education and Training as Investment
docs.text:
Human capital is the stock of skills, education, training, and experience embodied in workers that raises their productivity (\(MP_L\)) and therefore their MRP and wages. Human capital theory treats education and training as an investment decision, analogous to a firm's capital investment decision in Section 11.7: incur a cost now (tuition, foregone wages while studying) in exchange for higher earnings later.

A rational worker invests in education as long as the present value of the additional future earnings exceeds the cost of acquiring the education:

\[PV(\text{additional lifetime earnings}) > \text{Cost of education (tuition + foregone wages)}\]

The college decision as human capital investment

A student forgoes four years of full-time wages (say $35,000/year = $140,000 total opportunity cost) and pays tuition (say $40,000) to earn a college degree, for a total cost of $180,000. If the degree raises her expected lifetime earnings by a present value of $500,000, human capital theory predicts she should make the investment — the returns substantially exceed the costs.

docs.title: Why Does Education Raise Wages?
docs.text:
Two leading explanations exist, and they are not mutually exclusive:

  1. Human capital (productivity) view: Education directly raises a worker's skills and productivity (\(MP_L\)), raising MRP and therefore wages.
  2. Signaling view: Education may not raise productivity much directly, but completing a rigorous degree signals to employers that a worker is capable, disciplined, and intelligent — traits employers cannot observe directly but value highly.

Both views predict that educated workers earn more; they differ on why, with important policy implications for how much a given investment in education will raise economy-wide productivity versus merely reshuffling who gets which job.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Derived Demand Demand for an input that arises from demand for the output it helps produce Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) The additional revenue from employing one more unit of an input; \(MRP_L = MP_L \times MR\) Marginal Product of Labor (\(MP_L\)) The additional output produced by one more unit of labor Hiring Rule A firm hires an input up to the point where $MRP = $ input price Labor Demand Curve Equivalent to the MRP curve; shows quantity of labor demanded at each wage Work-Leisure Trade-off The decision of how to divide time between paid labor and unpaid leisure Substitution Effect (labor supply) A higher wage raises the opportunity cost of leisure, inducing more work Income Effect (labor supply) A higher wage raises income, inducing more leisure (fewer hours worked) Backward-Bending Labor Supply An individual supply curve that slopes up then bends backward at high wages Monopsony A market with a single (or dominant) buyer of an input Marginal Cost of Labor (MCL) The monopsonist's true marginal cost of hiring one more worker, exceeding the wage Interest Rate (\(r\)) The price of loanable funds; the cost of financing capital investment Present Value (PV) The value today of a future payment, discounted at the interest rate Economic Rent Payment to a factor in fixed supply, determined purely by demand Human Capital The stock of skills, education, and experience that raises worker productivity

docs.title: Problem 1 — Marginal Revenue Product
docs.text:
A furniture shop sells chairs at a competitive price of \(P = \$60\). Labor is the only variable input.

Workers Total Chairs/Week \(MP_L\) \(MRP_L\) 1 10 — — 2 18 — — 3 24 — — 4 28 — —

a) Fill in the \(MP_L\) and \(MRP_L\) columns. b) If the wage is $360/week, how many workers should the shop hire? c) If the wage falls to $240/week, how many workers should the shop hire?

Solution

a)

Workers Total Chairs \(MP_L\) \(MRP_L\) 1 10 10 $600 2 18 8 $480 3 24 6 $360 4 28 4 $240

b) At \(w = \$360\): hire up to where \(MRP_L \geq w\). \(MRP_L = \$360\) at the 3rd worker, and $240 < $360 at the 4th worker, so hire 3 workers.

c) At \(w = \$240\): \(MRP_L = \$240\) at the 4th worker, which just covers the wage, so hire 4 workers.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Labor Market Equilibrium
docs.text:
The labor market for registered nurses in a metro area is described by:

\[L^d = 5000 - 100w \qquad L^s = 500 + 150w\]

a) Find the equilibrium wage and employment level. b) If a new nursing school graduates an additional cohort, shifting labor supply to \(L^s = 1000 + 150w\), find the new equilibrium. c) Explain intuitively why the wage changed as it did.

Solution

a) Set \(L^d = L^s\): \(5000 - 100w = 500 + 150w \Rightarrow 4500 = 250w \Rightarrow w^* = \$18, \; L^* = 5000 - 100(18) = 3200\).

b) Set \(5000 - 100w = 1000 + 150w \Rightarrow 4000 = 250w \Rightarrow w^* = \$16, \; L^* = 5000 - 100(16) = 3400\).

c) Labor supply shifted right (more nurses available at every wage), creating a temporary surplus at the old wage of $18. The wage falls to $16 to clear the market, and equilibrium employment rises from 3200 to 3400.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Monopsony
docs.text:
A monopsonist coal mine is the only employer in an isolated town. It faces labor supply \(w = 15 + 0.01L\) and has \(MRP_L = 95 - 0.02L\).

a) Derive the marginal cost of labor (MCL) curve. b) Find the profit-maximizing level of employment. c) Find the wage the monopsonist actually pays. d) Compare this wage to the value of the marginal worker's output (\(MRP_L\)) at that employment level, and explain the gap.

Solution

a) \(TLC = wL = (15 + 0.01L)L = 15L + 0.01L^2 \Rightarrow MCL = 15 + 0.02L\).

b) Set \(MRP_L = MCL\): \(95 - 0.02L = 15 + 0.02L \Rightarrow 80 = 0.04L \Rightarrow L^* = 2000\).

c) \(w^* = 15 + 0.01(2000) = \$35\).

d) \(MRP_L\) at \(L = 2000\) is \(95 - 0.02(2000) = \$55\). The monopsonist pays workers $35 but each generates $55 in value — a $20 gap per worker. This gap is the essence of monopsony power: because the firm is the only buyer, it can pay workers less than their marginal contribution to revenue, and it also hires fewer workers than a competitive market would.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Present Value and Investment
docs.text:
A firm is considering a machine costing $50,000 today. It will produce a single payoff of $58,000 one year from now.

a) If the interest rate is 8%, should the firm buy the machine? Show the present value calculation. b) If the interest rate rises to 20%, should the firm buy the machine? c) Explain, in words, why rising interest rates reduce investment.

Solution

a) \(PV = \dfrac{58{,}000}{1.08} = \$53{,}703.70\). Since \(PV > \$50{,}000\) cost, the firm should buy the machine (positive NPV of $3,703.70).

b) \(PV = \dfrac{58{,}000}{1.20} = \$48{,}333.33\). Since \(PV < \$50{,}000\) cost, the firm should not buy the machine (negative NPV of -$1,666.67).

c) A higher interest rate raises the opportunity cost of tying up funds in a project (or raises the cost of borrowing to finance it), so it discounts future payoffs more heavily. Projects that were profitable at a low interest rate become unprofitable at a higher one, so investment demand falls as interest rates rise.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Economic Rent
docs.text:
A unique beachfront lot can only be used for one restaurant. Three restaurant chains bid for the annual lease: Chain A values it at $200,000/year, Chain B at $150,000/year, Chain C at $90,000/year. The lot has no alternative use and costs the owner nothing to maintain.

a) What is the equilibrium annual lease payment, assuming competitive bidding? b) How much of this payment is economic rent? Explain why. c) Suppose a new highway exit dramatically increases foot traffic near the lot, raising each chain's valuation by $50,000. What happens to the rent, and why does supply play no role?

Solution

a) Competitive bidding drives the lease price up to the second-highest valuation (since Chain A will outbid Chain B by any amount up to $150,000, but has no reason to pay more than necessary to win) — approximately $150,000/year (the lot goes to Chain A at a price just above Chain B's valuation).

b) Because the lot's supply is fixed (there is exactly one such lot and no cost of maintaining it), the entire $150,000 payment is economic rent — it does not reflect any production cost, only the value of controlling a scarce resource.

c) All valuations rise by $50,000 (Chain A to $250,000, Chain B to $200,000), so the equilibrium rent rises to approximately $200,000/year. Supply plays no role because the lot's supply curve is vertical — the quantity of this specific lot cannot increase no matter how valuable it becomes; the entire effect of increased demand falls on price (rent), not quantity.

You Just Priced Every Factor of Production

Labor, capital, and land each have their own market, their own logic, and their own quirks — monopsony power, present value, fixed supply — and you worked through all of them. You can now explain why wages differ, why interest rates matter for investment, and why a beachfront lot commands a premium that has nothing to do with the cost of building on it.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 12: Market Failures, we step back from well-functioning competitive markets to examine why markets sometimes fail to deliver efficient outcomes — and what role government can play in response.

docs.title: Quiz: Factor Markets
docs.text: Test your understanding of derived demand, marginal revenue product, labor supply, monopsony, and capital and land markets with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does it mean that the demand for labor is a "derived demand"?
docs.text:
1. Labor demand is determined solely by government wage-setting policy
  2. Workers derive utility directly from the act of working itself
  3. Labor demand is unrelated to the market for the final good being produced
  4. The demand for labor arises from, and depends on, the demand for the output that labor helps produce
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Nobody hires a worker for the worker's own sake; firms demand labor because it helps produce an output they can sell, so the demand for labor is derived from the demand for that output. Option A invents a government role not part of the concept, option B misattributes the firm's motivation to the worker's own utility, and option C directly contradicts the defining feature of derived demand.

Concept Tested: Derived Demand

docs.title: 2. How is marginal revenue product (MRP) calculated for a competitive firm?
docs.text:
1. MRP equals the marginal product of labor multiplied by the market price of output
  2. MRP equals the wage rate divided by the marginal product of labor
  3. MRP equals average product multiplied by total revenue
  4. MRP equals total revenue divided by the number of workers employed
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Since \(MRP_L = MP_L \times MR\), and \(MR = P\) for a competitive firm, \(MRP_L = MP_L \times P\) — the extra output from one more worker valued at the market price. Option B inverts the relationship, option C confuses average product with marginal product and misuses total revenue, and option D describes an unrelated average measure rather than a marginal one.

Concept Tested: Marginal Revenue Product

docs.title: 3. What is "economic rent"?
docs.text:
1. The monthly payment a renter makes for an apartment
  2. The additional cost a monopsonist incurs from hiring one more worker
  3. A payment to a factor of production whose supply is fixed, determined entirely by demand since supply cannot respond
  4. The portion of a worker's wage attributable to human capital investment
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Economic rent is the payment to a factor like land whose supply is essentially fixed; because supply cannot respond to price, the entire market-clearing payment is determined by demand alone and counts as rent. Option A describes an everyday use of the word "rent" unrelated to the economic concept, option B describes marginal cost of labor instead, and option D describes a return to human capital investment, a distinct concept from rent on a fixed-supply factor.

Concept Tested: Economic Rent

docs.title: 4. According to the hiring rule for a profit-maximizing firm, why should a firm stop hiring additional workers once MRP falls below the wage?
docs.text:
1. Because at that point, the next worker would cost more than the additional revenue they generate, reducing profit
  2. Because labor laws require firms to stop hiring once a certain wage threshold is reached
  3. Because marginal product always becomes negative once MRP falls below the wage
  4. Because firms must always hire the same number of workers as their competitors
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The hiring rule, \(MRP_L = w\), is a marginal-benefit-equals-marginal-cost condition: once \(MRP_L < w\), hiring that worker would cost more (the wage) than it adds in revenue (MRP), reducing profit. Option B invents a legal requirement not part of the economic model, option C is false since marginal product can still be positive, just low, when MRP falls below the wage, and option D is an unrelated and unsupported claim about competitor behavior.

Concept Tested: Labor Hiring Rule

docs.title: 5. Why can an individual's labor supply curve bend backward at high wage levels?
docs.text:
1. Because the substitution effect always dominates at every wage level
  2. Because firms refuse to pay wages above a certain threshold
  3. Because higher wages always reduce a worker's marginal product
  4. Because past some wage level, the income effect of a higher wage (wanting more leisure as a normal good) can dominate the substitution effect (wanting to work more because leisure is now more costly), leading to fewer hours worked
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. At high wages, a worker may be rich enough that the income effect — wanting more leisure as income rises — outweighs the substitution effect of a higher opportunity cost of leisure, causing hours worked to fall even as the wage continues to rise. Option A describes the opposite of what produces a backward bend, option B introduces an unrelated firm-side constraint, and option C confuses the wage-setting mechanism with a worker's own productivity, which this model does not assume changes with the wage.

Concept Tested: Backward-Bending Labor Supply

docs.title: 6. Compared to a competitive labor market, how does monopsony affect wages and employment?
docs.text:
1. Monopsony raises both wages and employment above the competitive level
  2. Monopsony has no effect on wages or employment, since firms still face the same supply curve
  3. Monopsony results in a lower wage and fewer workers hired than in a competitive labor market
  4. Monopsony only affects employment, leaving the wage unchanged
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Because a monopsonist's marginal cost of labor exceeds the wage, it hires where \(MRP_L = MCL\) and then pays only the (lower) wage read off the supply curve, resulting in both fewer workers hired and a lower wage than the competitive outcome. Option A reverses the actual direction of the effect, option B ignores that the monopsonist, as the sole buyer, faces the upward-sloping supply curve directly rather than a flat market wage, and option D incorrectly claims only one variable is affected when both wage and employment fall.

Concept Tested: Monopsony

docs.title: 7. A firm sells output at a competitive price of $8. The marginal product of the 5th worker is 15 units, the 6th worker is 10 units, and the 7th worker is 5 units. If the market wage is $70 per week, how many of these three additional workers (5th, 6th, and 7th) should the firm hire?
docs.text:
1. All three workers (5th, 6th, and 7th)
  2. Only the 5th and 6th workers
  3. Only the 5th worker
  4. None of the three workers
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. \(MRP_5 = 15\times\$8=\$120\), \(MRP_6=10\times\$8=\$80\), and \(MRP_7=5\times\$8=\$40\); the firm hires any worker whose MRP is at least the \(70 wage, so it hires the 5th (\)120\geq70\() and 6th (\)80\geq70\(), but not the 7th (\)40<70$). Option A incorrectly includes the unprofitable 7th worker, option C stops one worker short of the profitable hires, and option D wrongly excludes workers whose MRP clearly exceeds the wage.

Concept Tested: Marginal Revenue Product

docs.title: 8. The labor market for dental hygienists is described by \(L^d = 3000 - 50w\) and \(L^s = 600 + 100w\). What is the equilibrium wage?
docs.text:
1. $12
  2. $14
  3. $16
  4. $18
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Setting \(L^d=L^s\) gives \(3000-50w=600+100w \implies 2400=150w \implies w^*=\$16\). The other options result from arithmetic slips when combining the coefficients or constants on each side of the equation.

Concept Tested: Labor Market Equilibrium

docs.title: 9. A firm can buy a machine today for $20,000 that will generate a single payoff of $23,000 one year from now. If the interest rate is 12%, what is the present value of the payoff, and should the firm buy the machine?
docs.text:
1. PV ≈ $20,536; buy the machine, since PV exceeds its cost
  2. PV ≈ $25,760; do not buy the machine, since PV exceeds its cost
  3. PV ≈ $18,500; do not buy the machine, since PV is below its cost
  4. PV ≈ $23,000; buy the machine, since PV equals its future payoff
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. \(PV = \dfrac{23{,}000}{1.12} \approx \$20{,}536\), which exceeds the $20,000 cost, so the machine has a positive net present value and the firm should buy it. Option B multiplies instead of discounting, option C understates the present value and also contradicts itself by rejecting a project whose PV it claims exceeds cost, and option D incorrectly treats present value as equal to the undiscounted future payoff.

Concept Tested: Present Value

docs.title: 10. In a monopsony labor market, a policymaker proposes a minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage. Based on the chapter's analysis, what is the likely effect of this policy?
docs.text:
1. It would reduce both the wage and employment further below the monopsony outcome
  2. It would increase both the wage and employment, moving the market closer to the competitive outcome, unlike the typical effect of a minimum wage in a competitive labor market
  3. It would have no effect, since monopsonists always pay the competitive wage already
  4. It would increase the wage but necessarily create unemployment, exactly as a minimum wage would in a competitive labor market
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In a pure monopsony model, a minimum wage set in this range forces the monopsonist closer to the competitive hiring rule, which can raise both the wage and employment simultaneously — a result that would not occur under a minimum wage imposed on an already-competitive labor market. Option A describes the opposite of the documented effect, option C is false since a monopsonist's wage is below the competitive level by definition, and option D incorrectly imports the competitive-market logic (where a binding minimum wage creates a surplus of workers) into the monopsony case, where it does not apply in the same way.

Concept Tested: Monopsony Hiring Rule

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the conditions required for competitive markets to be efficient, and identify when those conditions break down
  2. Distinguish negative and positive externalities and explain why each leads markets away from the efficient outcome
  3. Define public goods and common-pool resources using the non-excludability and non-rivalry criteria, and explain the free-rider problem and the tragedy of the commons
  4. Explain how information asymmetry can cause markets to fail, including adverse selection and moral hazard
  5. Explain how market power causes inefficiency distinct from the other sources of market failure
  6. Compare taxes, regulation, property rights, and public provision as government responses to market failure
  7. Explain the concept of government failure and why government intervention does not automatically fix market failures

When the Invisible Hand Needs a Nudge

Every choice has a trade-off — and so far this book has mostly shown you markets getting that trade-off right on their own. This chapter is about the cases where they don't: pollution nobody pays for, goods nobody can be excluded from, deals where one side knows something the other doesn't. Understanding exactly why a market fails is the first step toward knowing whether — and how — to fix it.

docs.title: 12.1 When Do Markets Fail?
docs.text:
Chapter 2 showed that competitive markets, left alone, maximize total surplus — they are allocatively efficient. This is sometimes called the First Welfare Theorem: under certain conditions, competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient. But those conditions are demanding, and in the real world they frequently do not hold. A market failure occurs whenever the free market, on its own, fails to allocate resources efficiently — that is, whenever the price system does not lead to the surplus-maximizing quantity.

The conditions required for market efficiency — and the ways each can break down — are summarized below. This chapter surveys each category at a broad level; Chapter 13 returns to externalities and public goods in much greater depth.

Required Condition for Efficiency What Happens When It Fails Market Failure Category All costs and benefits are borne by buyers and sellers Costs/benefits spill onto third parties Externalities Goods are excludable and rival Goods can be consumed free, or use by one prevents use by others Public goods / common-pool resources Buyers and sellers have equal, sufficient information One side knows more than the other Information asymmetry Many small buyers and sellers, no one with pricing power A single firm (or few firms) controls price Market power

Efficiency is the benchmark, not a guarantee

None of these conditions is guaranteed to hold. Markets for haircuts, running shoes, and most restaurant meals come close to satisfying all four and function efficiently without intervention. Markets for pollution, lighthouses, vaccines, and used cars do not — and that is precisely where this chapter focuses.

Efficiency Was Never Magic — It Was a Checklist

Here's the mental model for this whole chapter: the First Welfare Theorem holds only when all four conditions in that table hold at once. Every topic between here and Section 12.6 is really just "which line of the checklist failed, and what does that specific failure look like?"

docs.title: 12.2 Externalities: Negative and Positive
docs.text: An externality exists when a transaction between a buyer and seller imposes costs or benefits on a third party who is not part of that transaction and whose interests are not reflected in the market price.

docs.title: Negative Externalities
docs.text:
A negative externality imposes a cost on third parties. The classic example is pollution: a factory's private cost of production does not include the cost of the air pollution it imposes on nearby residents. Because the firm does not pay for this cost, its private marginal cost curve lies below the true social marginal cost curve, and the market produces more than the efficient quantity.

\[\text{Social Marginal Cost} = \text{Private Marginal Cost} + \text{External Cost}\]

docs.title: Positive Externalities
docs.text:
A positive externality generates a benefit for third parties. Education is a common example: when you get vaccinated or become more educated, you benefit personally, but society also gains (lower disease transmission, a more informed citizenry, higher productivity of coworkers) in ways the market price does not capture. Because the market ignores this external benefit, the market produces less than the efficient quantity.

\[\text{Social Marginal Benefit} = \text{Private Marginal Benefit} + \text{External Benefit}\]

Everyday externalities

  • Negative: A loud late-night party (noise imposed on neighbors); a factory dumping waste in a river (harm to downstream users); vehicle emissions (climate and health costs borne by everyone).
  • Positive: A beekeeper's bees pollinating a neighboring orchard; a homeowner's beautiful garden raising neighborhood property values; getting a flu vaccine (reduces the chance others get sick).

Chapter 13 develops the full graphical and mathematical apparatus — including Pigouvian taxes, the Coase theorem, and cap-and-trade — for correcting externalities. For now, the key takeaway is the direction of the distortion: negative externalities cause overproduction, positive externalities cause underproduction, relative to the socially efficient level.

docs.title: 12.3 Public Goods: Non-Excludable, Non-Rival
docs.text:
Economists classify goods along two independent dimensions:

  • Excludable: Can the seller prevent people who do not pay from consuming the good?
  • Rival: Does one person's consumption reduce the amount available for others?
Rival Non-Rival Excludable Private goods (a sandwich, a haircut) Club goods (cable TV, a gym membership) Non-Excludable Common-pool resources (ocean fisheries, groundwater) Public goods (national defense, basic research, lighthouses)

Two Yes/No Questions, Four Boxes, No Ambiguity

Here's a fast way to classify any good on an exam: ask two questions in order. "Can the seller stop a non-payer from using it?" settles excludability. "Does my use leave less for you?" settles rivalry. Two yes/no answers drop you straight into the right box of that table.

A pure public good is both non-excludable (you cannot stop someone from consuming it even if they do not pay) and non-rival (one person's use does not diminish another's). National defense is the textbook example: protecting the country protects every resident, whether or not they paid taxes toward it, and one additional resident being "defended" does not reduce the defense available to anyone else.

Because no one can be excluded from enjoying a public good, private firms generally cannot profitably produce it — people have an incentive to free ride, consuming the benefit without paying. This is why public goods are typically funded through taxation and provided by government. Chapter 13 develops the free-rider problem and voting mechanisms for public goods provision in detail.

docs.title: 12.4 Common-Pool Resources and the Tragedy of the Commons
docs.text:
A common-pool resource is rival (one person's use depletes what is available to others) but non-excludable (no one can easily be stopped from using it). Ocean fisheries, groundwater aquifers, and unregulated grazing land are classic examples.

Same 'Non-Excludable' Label, Opposite Problem

Don't let the shared "non-excludable" label fool you into treating public goods and common-pool resources as the same problem. A public good (Section 12.3) is non-rival — my use doesn't reduce yours, so underfunding is the danger, not overuse. A common-pool resource is rival — which is exactly what makes overuse, not underfunding, the central threat here.

The tragedy of the commons describes what happens when a resource is open to all: because no individual user bears the full cost of their own extraction (part of that cost — the depleted resource — is spread across all other users), each person has a private incentive to overuse the resource even though collectively everyone would be better off with restraint. The result is systematic overexploitation and, in extreme cases, collapse of the resource.

Historical and modern tragedies of the commons

  • Atlantic cod fisheries: Decades of unrestricted fishing collapsed cod stocks off Newfoundland in the early 1990s, devastating an industry that had operated for centuries.
  • Groundwater aquifers: Farmers pumping from a shared aquifer have no individual incentive to conserve, since water they leave in the ground may simply be pumped by a neighbor instead.
  • Traffic congestion: Each additional driver on a congested highway imposes delay on all other drivers but bears only a small fraction of that cost personally.

Chapter 13 revisits common-pool resources with specific policy tools (catch shares, water rights, congestion pricing).

docs.title: 12.5 Information Asymmetry
docs.text: Information asymmetry exists when one party to a transaction has more or better information than the other. This can prevent markets from reaching efficient outcomes even when goods are perfectly rival, excludable, and free of externalities.

docs.title: Adverse Selection
docs.text: Adverse selection occurs when the party with less information ends up disproportionately transacting with the "worse" types from the other side, because information about quality is hidden before the transaction. The classic case is George Akerlof's "market for lemons": in a used-car market, sellers know whether their car is reliable or a "lemon," but buyers cannot tell. Buyers, unwilling to pay top price for a car that might be a lemon, offer only an average price — which then drives owners of genuinely good cars out of the market, leaving a disproportionate share of lemons for sale.

docs.title: Moral Hazard
docs.text:
Moral hazard occurs when one party changes their behavior after a transaction in ways the other party cannot observe or verify, because they no longer bear the full consequences of that behavior. A driver with comprehensive insurance may drive somewhat less carefully than an uninsured driver, since the insurer — not the driver — bears most of the cost of an accident.

Before the Deal, or After It? That's the Whole Distinction

Notice that timing is the entire difference between these two ideas: adverse selection is about hidden information before the deal is struck (who you're really dealing with), while moral hazard is about hidden behavior after the deal is struck (what they do once the incentives change). Ask yourself "before or after the contract?" and you'll never mix the two up again.

Looking ahead

Adverse selection and moral hazard, along with signaling and screening as partial solutions, are developed fully in Chapter 14: Information Economics.

docs.title: 12.6 Market Power as a Source of Failure
docs.text:
Chapters 7–9 showed that monopoly, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly all involve firms with some ability to set price above marginal cost. This market power is itself a distinct source of inefficiency, separate from externalities, public goods, or information problems.

A monopolist restricts output below the competitive level to raise price, creating deadweight loss: transactions that would make both the firm and some consumers better off simply do not happen, because the monopolist's profit-maximizing quantity is lower than the surplus-maximizing quantity.

\[Q_{monopoly} < Q_{competitive} \implies \text{Deadweight Loss} > 0\]

Unlike externalities, this failure does not require any third party at all — it can occur in a two-party market with no spillovers whatsoever, simply because the seller is not a price-taker. Policy responses include antitrust enforcement, price regulation of natural monopolies, and encouraging entry.

Quantifying the deadweight loss from market power

A market has demand \(P = 100 - Q\) and constant marginal cost \(MC = 20\) (the same cost a competitive industry would face).

Competitive outcome: Price-taking firms produce until \(P = MC\): \(100 - Q = 20 \implies Q_{competitive} = 80\).

Monopoly outcome: A monopolist produces until \(MR = MC\). With linear demand \(P = 100 - Q\), marginal revenue is \(MR = 100 - 2Q\). Setting \(MR = MC\):

\[100 - 2Q = 20 \implies Q_{monopoly} = 40, \qquad P_{monopoly} = 100 - 40 = \$60\]

The monopolist restricts output from 80 units to 40 units and raises price from $20 to $60. The deadweight loss is the triangle between the demand curve and \(MC\), between \(Q_{monopoly}\) and \(Q_{competitive}\):

\[DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (Q_{competitive} - Q_{monopoly}) \times (P_{monopoly} - MC) = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 40 = \$800\]

This $800 of surplus is destroyed — not transferred to anyone — purely because output is restricted below the efficient level. Chapter 7 develops this result in full.

docs.title: 12.7 Government Responses to Market Failure
docs.text:
Governments have four broad policy tools for addressing market failures. The right tool depends on which type of failure is present.

Policy Tool Best Suited For Example Taxes (Pigouvian) Negative externalities Carbon tax, cigarette tax Subsidies Positive externalities Vaccine subsidies, R&D tax credits Regulation Externalities, market power, information gaps Emissions standards, mandatory product labeling Property rights Common-pool resources Fishing quotas, tradable water rights Public provision Public goods National defense, public roads, basic research funding Antitrust enforcement Market power Breaking up or blocking anticompetitive mergers

Matching the tool to the failure

A city with heavy traffic congestion (a common-pool resource problem — roads are rival but hard to exclude people from) might use congestion pricing (a form of Pigouvian tax) rather than an R&D subsidy, which would do nothing to address the externality. Conversely, underfunded basic scientific research (a public good with positive externalities) is better addressed through direct public funding than through a tax, since the problem is underprovision, not overprovision.

docs.title: 12.8 Government Failure
docs.text: Government intervention is not automatically an improvement over the market outcome. Government failure occurs when a policy intended to correct a market failure instead makes outcomes worse, or fails to improve them, due to poor information, political incentives, or unintended side effects.

docs.title: Rent-Seeking
docs.text: Rent-seeking is the use of resources to obtain a larger share of existing wealth through the political process, rather than by creating new wealth. Firms may lobby for tariffs, subsidies, or regulations that benefit them specifically, at a cost borne by consumers or taxpayers generally. Because the benefits of rent-seeking are concentrated on a small group (who have a strong incentive to lobby) while the costs are spread across many people (each of whom has little individual incentive to oppose it), rent-seeking policies can persist even when they reduce total surplus.

docs.title: Other Sources of Government Failure
docs.text:
• Imperfect information: Regulators often know less about industry-specific conditions than the firms they regulate.
  • Principal-agent problems: Elected officials and bureaucrats may pursue their own re-election or budget-maximizing incentives rather than the public interest.
  • Unintended consequences: A policy designed to fix one problem may create new distortions elsewhere (e.g., a price ceiling intended to help consumers can create shortages, as seen in Chapter 2's extensions).
  • Regulatory capture: Regulated industries may come to influence or control the agencies meant to regulate them.

Market failure does not imply government success

The existence of a market failure is a necessary but not sufficient condition for government intervention to improve welfare. Economists compare the costs of the market failure against the costs of likely government failure before recommending intervention — sometimes "do nothing" is still the best available option.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Market Failure A situation in which the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently Externality A cost or benefit of a transaction that falls on a third party Negative Externality An external cost; leads to market overproduction Positive Externality An external benefit; leads to market underproduction Excludability Whether non-payers can be prevented from consuming a good Rivalry Whether one person's consumption reduces what is available to others Public Good A good that is both non-excludable and non-rival Common-Pool Resource A good that is rival but non-excludable Tragedy of the Commons Overexploitation of a shared resource because no user bears its full cost Information Asymmetry One party to a transaction has more/better information than the other Adverse Selection Hidden information before a transaction skews the market toward "worse" types Moral Hazard Hidden behavior after a transaction changes incentives because consequences are shared Market Power A firm's ability to set price above marginal cost, causing deadweight loss Pigouvian Tax A tax designed to correct a negative externality Rent-Seeking Using resources to capture existing wealth via politics rather than create new wealth Government Failure A policy intervention that fails to improve, or worsens, an inefficient outcome

docs.title: Problem 1 — Classifying Market Failures
docs.text:
For each scenario, identify the primary type of market failure (externality, public good/common-pool resource, information asymmetry, or market power).

a) A pharmaceutical company is the sole producer of a patented life-saving drug and charges a price far above its marginal cost. b) A chemical plant discharges waste into a river used by downstream fishing communities. c) A health insurance applicant knows about a pre-existing condition that the insurer cannot easily verify. d) A small town's fireworks display can be watched by everyone in town, whether or not they contributed to pay for it.

Solution

a) Market power — a single seller with no competition sets price above marginal cost, independent of any externality or information problem.

b) Negative externality — the plant's private cost of production does not include the harm imposed on downstream users.

c) Information asymmetry (adverse selection) — the applicant has hidden information about their own risk that the insurer lacks.

d) Public good — the fireworks display is non-excludable (anyone in town can watch) and non-rival (one person watching does not reduce what others see), creating a free-rider problem for funding it.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Excludability and Rivalry
docs.text:
Classify each good into one of the four categories (private good, club good, common-pool resource, public good) based on excludability and rivalry, and justify your answer.

a) A Netflix subscription b) Open-ocean tuna stocks c) A slice of pizza d) Street lighting on a public road

Solution

a) Club good — excludable (you need a paid subscription), non-rival (your friend watching doesn't reduce your access).

b) Common-pool resource — non-excludable (hard to stop anyone from fishing international waters), rival (fish caught by one boat are unavailable to others).

c) Private good — excludable (the seller can refuse to give it to you without payment) and rival (once you eat it, no one else can).

d) Public good — non-excludable (anyone walking the street benefits from the light) and non-rival (one pedestrian benefiting doesn't reduce the light available to another).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Matching Policy to Failure
docs.text:
For each market failure below, recommend the most appropriate government response from Section 12.7 (tax, subsidy, regulation, property rights, public provision, or antitrust) and briefly justify your choice.

a) Overfishing in a shared coastal fishery. b) A factory emitting air pollution with no regulation. c) Underfunded basic scientific research with broad social spillover benefits. d) A proposed merger between the only two firms in a local cable market.

Solution

a) Property rights (e.g., individual transferable fishing quotas) — assigning each fisher an enforceable share of the total allowable catch gives them a private incentive to conserve the resource's long-run value, directly addressing the common-pool resource problem.

b) Pigouvian tax or regulation (e.g., an emissions tax or an emissions cap) — forces the factory to internalize the external cost of its pollution, or legally limits the externality directly.

c) Subsidy or public provision — since the social benefit of research exceeds the private benefit captured by the researcher, the government should subsidize or directly fund research to increase it toward the efficient level.

d) Antitrust enforcement (block or restrict the merger) — combining the only two firms would create a monopoly, which would restrict output and raise prices; antitrust review protects against this specific type of market-power failure.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Government Failure
docs.text:
A city government, concerned about a shortage of affordable housing (which it attributes to market failure), imposes strict rent control, capping rents well below the market-clearing level.

a) Is a shortage of affordable housing, by itself, necessarily evidence of a market failure? Explain. b) Using the supply-and-demand framework from Chapter 2, predict the effect of the rent cap on the quantity of housing supplied and demanded. c) Explain how this policy could be an example of government failure.

Solution

a) Not necessarily. High rents might simply reflect high demand relative to a scarce resource (land in a desirable location) rather than any failure of the market mechanism itself — the market may be functioning efficiently even though the equilibrium price is high. A true market failure would require, e.g., an externality, information problem, or market power specific to the housing market (such as zoning-driven monopoly power among developers).

b) A rent cap set below the equilibrium rent creates a shortage: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the capped price, exactly as in Chapter 2's price-ceiling analysis. Landlords have less incentive to maintain or build new rental housing, and more renters want apartments than are available.

c) This is a textbook case of government failure: a policy intended to make housing more "affordable" instead reduces the quantity supplied, worsens the shortage, and can lead to under-maintenance of existing units and inefficient allocation of apartments (e.g., to those with longest tenure rather than greatest need) — the intervention makes the underlying problem worse rather than correcting a genuine market failure.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Market Power and Deadweight Loss
docs.text:
A city grants an exclusive franchise to a single cable provider. Market demand for cable service is \(P = 80 - Q\), and the constant marginal cost of providing service is \(MC = 20\).

a) Find the quantity and price that would prevail if the market were competitive (\(P = MC\)). b) Find the monopolist's profit-maximizing quantity and price (recall \(MR = 80 - 2Q\) for linear demand \(P = 80 - Q\)). c) Calculate the deadweight loss created by the exclusive franchise. d) Suppose a lobbying firm could spend up to the entire gain in monopoly profit to keep the franchise exclusive. Relate this to the concept of rent-seeking from Section 12.8.

Solution

a) \(80 - Q = 20 \implies Q_{competitive} = 60, \; P_{competitive} = \$20\).

b) Set \(MR = MC\): \(80 - 2Q = 20 \implies Q_{monopoly} = 30, \; P_{monopoly} = 80 - 30 = \$50\).

c) \(DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (60 - 30) \times (50 - 20) = \frac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 30 = \$450\).

d) The monopolist's profit from the franchise is \((P_{monopoly} - MC) \times Q_{monopoly} = (50-20) \times 30 = \$900\) above the competitive (zero-profit) benchmark. Because this $900 is a prize created purely by restricting entry, the firm (or a lobbyist acting for it) has an incentive to spend resources — up to nearly $900 — on lobbying to preserve the exclusive franchise. Those lobbying expenditures produce no new goods or services; they are pure rent-seeking, and the resources spent on them are a further social loss layered on top of the original $450 deadweight loss from restricted output.

You Can Now Diagnose Why a Market Is Failing

Externalities, public goods, information asymmetry, market power, and even the ways government intervention can backfire — you worked through every major category economists use to explain why markets don't always deliver efficient outcomes on their own. That diagnostic skill is exactly what Chapter 13 builds on, going deep on the tools that fix externalities and fund public goods.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 13: Externalities and Public Goods, we return to externalities and public goods in much greater depth — deriving the Pigouvian tax mathematically, working through the Coase theorem, and analyzing cap-and-trade and public-goods voting mechanisms.

docs.title: Quiz: Market Failures
docs.text: Test your understanding of externalities, public goods, information asymmetry, market power, and government responses to market failure with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a "market failure"?
docs.text:
1. Any situation in which a firm earns zero economic profit in the long run
  2. A situation in which the free market, on its own, fails to allocate resources efficiently
  3. A government policy that reduces total surplus
  4. Any market where price is above marginal cost temporarily
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A market failure occurs whenever the free market fails to produce the surplus-maximizing (efficient) quantity on its own, typically because one of the conditions behind the First Welfare Theorem breaks down. Option A describes a normal, efficient long-run competitive outcome, option C describes government failure instead, and option D describes a feature of market power specifically, not market failure in general.

Concept Tested: Market Failure

docs.title: 2. What is an "externality"?
docs.text:
1. A cost or benefit of a transaction that falls on a third party not involved in that transaction
  2. The difference between a firm's accounting profit and economic profit
  3. A tax imposed directly on the buyer or seller in a transaction
  4. The portion of consumer surplus captured by a monopolist
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An externality exists when a transaction's costs or benefits spill onto someone who is not a party to that transaction and whose interests the market price does not reflect, such as pollution harming nearby residents. Option B describes a cost-accounting distinction unrelated to spillovers, option C describes a government policy tool rather than the market failure itself, and option D describes a transfer under market power, a separate category of failure.

Concept Tested: Externality

docs.title: 3. Which combination of criteria defines a "public good"?
docs.text:
1. Excludable and rival
  2. Excludable and non-rival
  3. Non-excludable and rival
  4. Non-excludable and non-rival
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A public good is both non-excludable (no one can be stopped from consuming it, even without paying) and non-rival (one person's use doesn't reduce what's available to others), as with national defense. Option A describes a private good, option B describes a club good, and option C describes a common-pool resource.

Concept Tested: Public Good

docs.title: 4. Why does a negative externality cause a market to overproduce relative to the efficient quantity?
docs.text:
1. Because the private marginal cost curve lies below the true social marginal cost curve, so firms produce beyond the point where social marginal cost equals social marginal benefit
  2. Because the private marginal benefit curve lies above the social marginal benefit curve
  3. Because negative externalities always eliminate consumer surplus entirely
  4. Because firms deliberately ignore their own private costs
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Since social marginal cost equals private marginal cost plus the external cost, a firm that ignores the external cost treats its (lower) private marginal cost as if it were the full cost, leading it to produce more than the socially efficient quantity. Option B misapplies the externality to the benefit side when the externality here is on the cost side, option C overstates the effect since consumer surplus is reduced, not eliminated, and option D mischaracterizes the firm as ignoring costs it actually does pay, rather than costs borne by third parties.

Concept Tested: Negative Externality

docs.title: 5. What is the key timing distinction between adverse selection and moral hazard?
docs.text:
1. Adverse selection involves hidden information before a transaction, while moral hazard involves hidden behavior after a transaction
  2. Adverse selection occurs only in insurance markets, while moral hazard occurs only in labor markets
  3. Adverse selection involves government policy, while moral hazard involves private behavior
  4. There is no meaningful distinction; the two terms describe the same phenomenon
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Adverse selection concerns information hidden before a deal is struck (such as a used car's true quality), while moral hazard concerns behavior that changes after a deal is struck, once incentives shift (such as driving less carefully once insured). Option B wrongly restricts each concept to a single industry when both can appear across many markets, option C invents an unsupported government-versus-private distinction, and option D denies a well-established and meaningful difference.

Concept Tested: Adverse Selection

docs.title: 6. What causes the "tragedy of the commons" in a common-pool resource?
docs.text:
1. Because the resource is excludable, allowing the owner to overcharge users
  2. Because each user bears only part of the cost of their own extraction, while the rest is spread across all other users, creating an incentive to overuse the resource
  3. Because the resource is non-rival, so no one has an incentive to use it at all
  4. Because government regulation always prevents any use of the resource
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Because a common-pool resource is rival but non-excludable, each user ignores the cost their own extraction imposes on others (a depleted shared resource), leading to systematic overuse even though restraint would benefit everyone collectively. Option A incorrectly describes the resource as excludable, which is the opposite of the defining condition, option C misapplies rivalry (common-pool resources are rival, not non-rival), and option D invents a regulatory claim not part of the basic mechanism.

Concept Tested: Tragedy of the Commons

docs.title: 7. A city grants an exclusive franchise for local internet service. Market demand is \(P = 90 - Q\), and marginal cost is constant at \(MC = 10\). What is the deadweight loss created by this market-power-based market failure?
docs.text:
1. $400
  2. $800
  3. $1,600
  4. $3,200
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The competitive quantity is \(Q_C=80\) (where \(P=MC\)), and the monopoly quantity is \(Q_M=40\) (where \(MR=90-2Q=10\)), giving \(P_M=\$50\); the deadweight loss triangle is \(\frac{1}{2}\times(80-40)\times(50-10)=\frac{1}{2}\times40\times40=\$800\). The other options result from using only one of the two differences or from doubling instead of halving the triangle's area.

Concept Tested: Market Power as Failure

docs.title: 8. A city park is open to anyone, and no one can be charged for entering or stopped from enjoying it, while there is no limit on how many people can use it simultaneously without reducing enjoyment for others (within reason). How should this good be classified according to the excludability and rivalry criteria?
docs.text:
1. Private good, since it is excludable and rival
  2. Club good, since it is excludable but non-rival
  3. Common-pool resource, since it is non-excludable but rival
  4. Public good, since it is non-excludable and non-rival
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The park cannot exclude non-payers and one visitor's enjoyment does not reduce another's (up to reasonable capacity), matching the non-excludable, non-rival definition of a public good. Option A and B both incorrectly describe the park as excludable, which it is not, and option C incorrectly describes it as rival, when the scenario specifies that use does not meaningfully reduce availability to others.

Concept Tested: Public Good

docs.title: 9. A firm holds an exclusive government license worth $900 per year in monopoly profit above the competitive benchmark. Based on the concept of rent-seeking, what is the most the firm would rationally be willing to spend lobbying to preserve this license?
docs.text:
1. Nothing, since lobbying produces no new output
  2. Exactly $450, half of the monopoly profit
  3. Up to just under $900, the full value of the monopoly profit it is trying to protect
  4. An unlimited amount, since rent-seeking has no upper bound in theory
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Because the $900 is a prize created purely by restricting entry, a rational firm is willing to spend up to just under that full amount on lobbying, since doing so still leaves it better off than losing the license entirely. Option A ignores the real incentive firms have to protect valuable rents, option B invents an arbitrary fraction not implied by the rent-seeking logic, and option D is incorrect since spending more than the prize itself is worth would make the firm worse off than not lobbying at all.

Concept Tested: Rent-Seeking

docs.title: 10. A government imposes a price ceiling intending to correct a perceived market failure. Based on the chapter's discussion of government failure, under what condition would this intervention most likely make the problem worse rather than better?
docs.text:
1. When the government has perfect information about the market and no political constraints
  2. When the policy exactly offsets an existing negative externality
  3. When the original market was already perfectly competitive and efficient, so the price ceiling creates a shortage where none existed before
  4. When the market failure being addressed is a public good problem rather than a price-related one
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. If the market was already efficient, imposing a price ceiling introduces a shortage where none existed, exactly the kind of unintended side effect the chapter identifies as government failure — the existence of high prices alone is not proof of a genuine market failure. Option A describes conditions under which intervention is more likely to succeed, not fail, option B describes a case where the policy is well-matched to an actual failure, and option D describes mismatching the tool to the wrong failure type, a different issue from the scenario described.

Concept Tested: Government Failure

docs.title: References: Market Failures
docs.text:
1. Market failure - Wikipedia - Surveys the general conditions under which markets fail to allocate resources efficiently, matching the chapter's overview taxonomy of market failure categories.

  2. Externality - Wikipedia - Explains how costs or benefits can spill onto third parties, matching the chapter's negative- and positive-externality section.

  3. Information asymmetry - Wikipedia - Covers how unequal information between buyers and sellers can cause markets to fail, matching the chapter's adverse-selection and moral-hazard overview.

  4. "The Anatomy of Market Failure" - Francis M. Bator - Quarterly Journal of Economics (1958) - Bator's article coined the term "market failure" and built the taxonomy (externalities, public goods, information problems, market power) that structures this entire chapter.

  5. "The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure" - Paul A. Samuelson - Review of Economics and Statistics (1954) - Samuelson's efficiency condition for public-goods provision underlies the chapter's brief treatment of non-excludable, non-rival goods and the free-rider problem.

  6. Market failure and the role of government - Khan Academy - A unit covering externalities, public goods, and government responses to market failure, matching this chapter's survey structure.

  7. Market Failure - Investopedia - Defines market failure and lists its main causes with real-world examples, reinforcing the chapter's checklist-style approach.

  8. Public good - Wikipedia - Explains non-excludability and non-rivalry, the defining properties of public goods covered in the chapter's market-failure taxonomy.

  9. Asymmetric Information - Investopedia - Explains how one-sided information can prevent efficient trades, supporting the chapter's preview of adverse selection and moral hazard (expanded in Chapter 14).

  10. Rent-seeking - Wikipedia - Explains how individuals and firms expend resources lobbying for favorable regulation rather than creating value, illustrating the chapter's closing discussion of government failure.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Distinguish private (internal) costs and benefits from social costs and benefits, and identify the deadweight loss from negative and positive externalities
  2. Calculate the efficient output level and the optimal Pigouvian tax or subsidy for a market with an externality
  3. State the Coase theorem and work through a private-bargaining example to an efficient outcome
  4. Explain how cap-and-trade systems achieve efficient pollution reduction at least cost
  5. Define public goods and derive the condition for their efficient provision
  6. Explain the free-rider problem using a simple game-theoretic example
  7. Compare voting mechanisms for public-goods provision and analyze common-pool resource solutions (quotas, pricing, and property rights)

Welcome to Market Failure, Part II

Every choice has a trade-off! And that's true for markets too, even when the costs and benefits spill onto people who never agreed to the deal: the fishery downstream of a factory, the neighbor who benefits from your flu shot, everyone who enjoys a fireworks display they didn't pay for. By the end of this chapter, you'll have a toolkit -- Pigouvian taxes, Coasean bargains, cap-and-trade, and public-goods financing -- for nudging private incentives back in line with what's best for society as a whole.

docs.title: Private vs. Social Cost
docs.text:
When a firm's production imposes costs on third parties, the private marginal cost (PMC) that the firm pays diverges from the social marginal cost (SMC) borne by society as a whole:

\[SMC = PMC + MEC\]

where \(MEC\) is the marginal external cost imposed on third parties. Because the firm only considers \(PMC\), not \(SMC\), when deciding how much to produce, the market supply curve (which reflects \(PMC\)) lies below the true social cost curve.

The Wedge That Breaks Markets

Notice what's really going on here: the firm's supply curve was never wrong about the firm's own costs -- it's just answering the wrong question. Every externality problem in this chapter boils down to this same wedge between what a decision-maker pays (or receives) and what society as a whole pays (or receives). Once you can spot that wedge, you can predict which direction the market will miss the efficient outcome.

docs.title: Finding the Efficient Quantity
docs.text:
The market reaches its (private) equilibrium where private marginal cost equals private marginal benefit (\(PMC = PMB\), which for a competitive market is simply \(S = D\)). But the efficient quantity is where social marginal cost equals social marginal benefit: \(SMC = SMB\). Because \(SMC > PMC\) with a negative externality, the efficient quantity is always less than the market quantity.

Worked example: a steel mill polluting a river

A steel mill's private marginal cost is \(PMC = 2Q\), and demand (= private and social marginal benefit, since there's no externality on the buyer side) is \(P = 100 - Q\). The mill's pollution imposes a constant marginal external cost of \(MEC = 20\) per unit on a downstream fishery.

Market (unregulated) equilibrium: Set \(PMC = PMB\):

\[2Q = 100 - Q \implies 3Q = 100 \implies Q_{market} = 33.3, \quad P_{market} = \$66.67\]

Efficient quantity: \(SMC = PMC + MEC = 2Q + 20\). Set \(SMC = SMB\):

\[2Q + 20 = 100 - Q \implies 3Q = 80 \implies Q_{efficient} = 26.7\]

The market overproduces by \(33.3 - 26.7 = 6.6\) units relative to the efficient level.

docs.title: Deadweight Loss from a Negative Externality
docs.text:
Every unit produced beyond \(Q_{efficient}\) costs society more than it is worth (since \(SMC > SMB\) for \(Q > Q_{efficient}\)). The deadweight loss is the triangle between the \(SMC\) and \(SMB\) curves, from \(Q_{efficient}\) to \(Q_{market}\):

\[DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (Q_{market} - Q_{efficient}) \times MEC = \frac{1}{2} \times 6.6 \times 20 \approx \$66\]

Efficient Doesn't Mean Zero

A common trap: assuming the "efficient" response to pollution is to eliminate it entirely. It isn't -- \(Q_{efficient}\) in the steel mill example is still a healthy 26.7 units, not zero. The efficient quantity is wherever \(SMC = SMB\), and some pollution is efficient as long as the good produced is worth more than the social cost of making it.

docs.title: Private vs. Social Benefit
docs.text:
With a positive externality, the social marginal benefit (SMB) exceeds the private marginal benefit (PMB):

\[SMB = PMB + MEB\]

where \(MEB\) is the marginal external benefit enjoyed by third parties. Because buyers only consider their own \(PMB\), the market demand curve lies below the true social benefit curve, and the market underproduces relative to the efficient quantity.

Worked example: flu vaccinations

Private demand for flu shots is \(P = 60 - Q\) (reflecting each individual's own protection), and private marginal cost (= social marginal cost, since there's no externality on the supply side) is \(PMC = Q\). Vaccination generates a constant marginal external benefit of \(MEB = 10\) per unit (reduced disease transmission to others).

Market equilibrium: \(PMB = PMC \implies 60 - Q = Q \implies Q_{market} = 30\).

Efficient quantity: \(SMB = PMB + MEB = 60 - Q + 10 = 70 - Q\). Set \(SMB = SMC\):

\[70 - Q = Q \implies Q_{efficient} = 35\]

The market underproduces by \(35 - 30 = 5\) units of vaccination relative to the efficient level. The resulting deadweight loss is \(\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10 = \$25\).
